Part I

High Level

The big picture: what it is, why it exists, and how it works end to end.

1Foundations
1.1 · Foundations

Introduction

In one sentence

A NetworkPolicy is a namespaced Kubernetes object that says which pods a set of pods may talk to, and on which ports — everything else is dropped by the CNI.

Definition

📘 Formal definition

A NetworkPolicy is a namespaced Kubernetes resource (networking.k8s.io/v1) that selects a group of pods via a podSelector and declares an allow-list of ingress (incoming) and/or egress (outgoing) traffic at L3/L4 — using sources/destinations identified by pod labels, namespace labels, or IP CIDR blocks, restricted to specific TCP/UDP/SCTP ports.

It is part of the core Kubernetes API (networking.k8s.io/v1, stable since 1.7), maintained by SIG Network. Kubernetes only stores it; the cluster’s network plugin (CNI) enforces it on every node. You manage it with kubectl like any other object; its short name is netpol.

✓ It is
  • An allow-list per pod, for ingress and egress
  • Label-based: selects pods and namespaces by labels
  • Layer 3/4: IP addresses, protocols and ports
  • Namespaced: it only selects pods in its own namespace
  • Additive: all matching policies are combined with OR
  • Enforced by the CNI (VPC CNI agent, Calico, Cilium…)
✕ It is not
  • A deny list — v1 has no deny rule and no priority
  • Layer 7 — it cannot see HTTP paths, methods or hostnames
  • Cluster-wide — there is no “all namespaces” policy in v1
  • Authentication — it does not encrypt or prove identity (no mTLS)
  • A Service firewall — it filters pod IPs after the Service VIP is translated
  • Active on its own — without an enforcing CNI it does nothing

Definitions

🎯 Selected pod

The pods a policy protects, chosen by the policy’s podSelector from its own namespace.

🎯 Why it existsRules are written against labels, not IPs, so they keep working when pods move, scale or get new IPs.
📄 What it looks like
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
⚙ What the CNI does with itResolves the selector to the current pod IPs on every node, and re-resolves it whenever pods start or stop.
Before3 payments pods, no rules
→
After3 payment pods behind a per-pod firewall
📍 Where it livesspec.podSelector of a NetworkPolicy in jahez-prod.
⚠ Watch outpodSelector: {} selects every pod in the namespace — that is the default-deny trick, not a mistake.
🧱 Isolation

A pod becomes isolated for a direction (ingress or egress) the moment any policy selects it for that direction; then only listed traffic passes.

🎯 Why it existsIt turns Kubernetes’ default “everything may talk” into “nothing may talk unless allowed”, one pod and one direction at a time.
📄 What it looks like
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]   # no rules = deny all
⚙ What the CNI does with itSwitches the pod’s firewall default from ALLOW ANY to DENY ANY for that direction.
Beforeorders-svc → payments-db :5432 works
→
Afterorders-svc → payments-db times out
📍 Where it livesNot a field — a state of the pod, computed by the CNI from all policies that select it.
⚠ Watch outIsolation is per direction: a policy with only Ingress leaves the pod’s egress wide open.
↔ policyTypes

The list of directions this policy controls: Ingress, Egress, or both.

🎯 Why it existsIt says which side of the pod’s firewall the policy owns, even when the rule list for that side is empty.
📄 What it looks like
policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
⚙ What the CNI does with itMarks the selected pods as isolated for each listed direction.
Beforeegress open
→
Afteregress isolated
📍 Where it livesspec.policyTypes.
⚠ Watch outIf you omit it, Kubernetes guesses: Ingress always, Egress only when an egress section exists. Always write it.
⬇ Ingress rule

One entry in spec.ingress: who may connect in (from) and on which ports (ports).

🎯 Why it existsProtects the receiver — the database or service decides who may call it.
📄 What it looks like
ingress:
  - from:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
⚙ What the CNI does with itAdds “source set × port set” to the pod’s inbound allow-list.
Beforegateway → payments :8080 works
→
Afteronly orders → payments :8080 works
📍 Where it livesspec.ingress[].
⚠ Watch outingress: [{}] (one empty rule) allows everything; ingress: [] allows nothing.
⬆ Egress rule

One entry in spec.egress: where the pod may connect out (to) and on which ports.

🎯 Why it existsProtects everyone else from the pod — limits what a compromised container can reach or leak to.
📄 What it looks like
egress:
  - to:
      - ipBlock: { cidr: 203.0.113.0/24 }   # Mada (placeholder)
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]
⚙ What the CNI does with itAdds “destination set × port set” to the pod’s outbound allow-list.
Beforepayments → any internet host
→
Afterpayments → Mada :443 only
📍 Where it livesspec.egress[].
⚠ Watch outOnce egress is isolated, DNS breaks unless you also allow kube-dns on UDP and TCP 53.
👥 Peer

One item in a from or to list: pods by label, namespaces by label, both together, or an IP range (ipBlock).

🎯 Why it existsIt names the other side of the connection without hard-coding pod IPs.
📄 What it looks like
from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
    podSelector:
      matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
⚙ What the CNI does with itTurns the peer into a live IP set (pods) or a CIDR (ipBlock).
Beforeany pod in monitoring
→
Afteronly prometheus pods in monitoring
📍 Where it livesingress[].from[] and egress[].to[].
⚠ Watch outTwo keys in one item = AND. Two items (two dashes) = OR. One missing dash widens the rule silently.
🔌 Port

One item in a rule’s ports list: a protocol (TCP, UDP, SCTP) and a port number, named port or range.

🎯 Why it existsIt narrows an allowed peer to the one service port it actually needs.
📄 What it looks like
ports:
  - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
  - { protocol: TCP, port: 32000, endPort: 32767 }
⚙ What the CNI does with itAdds the port match to every peer of the same rule.
Beforeorders → orders-db any port
→
Afterorders → orders-db :5432 only
📍 Where it livesingress[].ports[] and egress[].ports[].
⚠ Watch outA rule with no ports allows all ports to its peers.
➕ Additive union

All policies that select a pod are combined with OR: the pod may do anything that any of them allows.

🎯 Why it existsTeams can add policies without breaking each other’s rules; there is no order or priority to manage.
📄 What it looks like
# default-deny-all-network-policy   → allows nothing
# payments-svc-network-policy        → allows orders :8080
# effective: orders :8080
⚙ What the CNI does with itMerges every matching rule into one allow-list per pod and direction.
Before2 policies, 2 lists
→
After1 merged allow-list
📍 Where it livesComputed by the CNI on each node.
⚠ Watch outYou cannot write a “deny” in v1. To block something, make sure no policy allows it.
🛡 Enforcer (CNI)

The network plugin that turns policies into kernel rules on every node. On Jahez EKS it is the AWS VPC CNI with its network-policy agent.

🎯 Why it existsThe API server only stores the YAML; without an enforcing CNI the policy does nothing.
📄 What it looks like
# aws-node DaemonSet, container aws-eks-nodeagent
# enabled with: enableNetworkPolicy: "true"
⚙ What the CNI does with itWatches policies and pods, compiles eBPF programs, attaches them to each pod’s network interface.
Beforepolicy stored in etcd
→
Afterpackets checked on the node
📍 Where it liveskube-system DaemonSet on every worker node; on EKS, a controller in the control plane too.
⚠ Watch outA CNI without policy support (Flannel alone, VPC CNI with the agent disabled) accepts your YAML and silently ignores it.
↩ Return traffic

Replies on a connection that was allowed are allowed automatically; the CNI tracks the connection (conntrack).

🎯 Why it existsYou describe who may start a connection, not every packet of it.
📄 What it looks like
# orders → payments :8080 allowed
# payments → orders (reply) needs no rule
⚙ What the CNI does with itMarks the flow ESTABLISHED and lets the reply packets through.
Beforereply needs a rule?
→
Afterreply passes on its own
📍 Where it livesKernel connection-tracking table on the node.
⚠ Watch outLong-lived connections opened before a policy change keep working until they close; test with new connections.
1.2 · Foundations

Problems or needs

In one sentence

A plain Kubernetes cluster is one flat network: any pod can open a connection to any other pod, any namespace and the internet, so one compromised container can reach everything.

The flat-network problem

The Kubernetes networking model has three rules:

  1. Every pod gets its own routable IP address.
  2. Every pod can communicate with every other pod, on every node, without NAT.
  3. An agent on the node (kubelet, system daemons) can reach all pods on that node.

This is by design — it makes the cluster feel like a single flat network and removes all the port-mapping complexity of Docker's bridge networking. But it has a security implication that hits hard the first time it bites you.

⚠️ The blast radius

If an attacker gets RCE in any pod — say, your image-processing worker via a libpng exploit — that pod can immediately open a TCP connection to:

  • Your Postgres pod's port 5432 in the databases namespace.
  • Your Redis pod's port 6379 with no auth (the default).
  • Your internal admin dashboard on :8080.
  • The cluster's metadata service at 169.254.169.254 (cloud IAM credentials).
  • Every other workload in every other namespace.

None of this requires DNS, certificates, or service accounts. Just a TCP connect() call.

Kubernetes ships default-allow

If no NetworkPolicy selects a given pod, that pod accepts all ingress traffic and can send all egress traffic. Kubernetes ships with default-allow.

The real cluster, step by step

Eight pods in jahez-prod and jahez-data: three service + database pairs (menu, orders, payments) behind one gateway. Payments is the most sensitive service: only orders should ever call it. Each step shows the problem and the manual commands that prove it.

Case 1 — BEFORE: no NetworkPolicy applied
1 / 6

What we want: user hits the gateway; the gateway dispatches to menu (browsing) or orders (checkout); each service uses its own DB; and orders — as part of a checkout — calls payments, which in turn writes to payments-db.

Step 3 — Problem A: gateway can reach any database directly

Because there is no policy, the gateway can open TCP :5432 directly to any of the three databases — completely bypassing the service tier that would normally authenticate and audit. One SSRF-style bug in the gateway = full database access.

Manual check — run it yourself
terminalbash
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod deploy/api-gateway-deployment -- nc -zv -w 3 orders-db.jahez-data 5432
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod deploy/api-gateway-deployment -- nc -zv -w 3 payments-db.jahez-data 5432

orders-db.jahez-data (172.20.12.40:5432) open      ← should be blocked
payments-db.jahez-data (172.20.12.77:5432) open    ← should be blocked

Step 4 — Problem B: payments-svc can reach orders-db

Payments should only touch its own database. But with no policy, a bug (or malicious plugin) in payments-svc can also connect to orders-db :5432 — read order history, modify totals, cross-contaminate two separate data domains. This is exactly the kind of blast-radius issue segmentation is meant to prevent.

Step 5 — Problem C: gateway or menu can call payments

Payments should only ever be invoked from orders (during checkout). But without a policy, both the gateway and the unrelated menu service can hit payments :8080 directly — and menu can also reach payments-db :5432. This is the widest blast radius yet: two unrelated services can charge cards or read the payment ledger.

1.3 · Foundations

Solution

In one sentence

Start every namespace with a policy that denies everything, allow DNS, then allow each real flow twice — as egress on the sender and ingress on the receiver.

The solution in steps

The solution in five steps — the order matters: deny first, then add back only what is needed

The three rules the solution relies on

Rule 2 — A pod with any policy flips to default-deny for that direction

The moment a pod is selected by at least one policy whose policyTypes includes Ingress, that pod's ingress flips to default-deny — only what is explicitly allowed by the union of all matching policies' ingress rules will work. Same independently for Egress.

The asymmetry trap. If you write a policy that only specifies policyTypes: [Ingress], the pod's egress stays default-allow. Many teams ship "secure" policies that lock down ingress while egress remains wide open — DNS exfil, anyone?

Rule 3 — Policies are purely additive (OR)

If three policies select the same pod, the effective allow-list is the union of all three. There is no concept of priority, ordering, or override. If any policy allows a flow, it's allowed.

Fig 3.1 — Multiple policies on the same pod: their allow-lists are unioned

The truth table

Pod selected by ingress policy?Pod selected by egress policy?Ingress behaviorEgress behavior
NoNoallow allallow all
YesNodeny except listedallow all
NoYesallow alldeny except listed
YesYesdeny except listeddeny except listed

Once you internalize this, the design pattern becomes obvious: start every namespace with a default-deny policy that selects everything, then layer narrow allow-rules on top. We use exactly this pattern in the Jahez project below.

Ingress closes the doors — the real cluster

The same eight pods. Ingress policies on the receivers close problems A, B (the database side) and C.

Case 2 — INGRESS policies on payments & every database
1 / 6

Step 1 — What ingress policies close

Ingress rules run at the destination pod's kernel: "who is allowed to arrive at me, on which port?". We install four:

  • payments-svc ingress — only orders-svc may reach it on :8080. Closes Problem C.
  • orders-db ingress — only orders-svc may reach it on :5432. Closes payments→orders-db (Problem B) and gateway→orders-db (part of Problem A).
  • payments-db ingress — only payments-svc may reach it on :5432. Closes menu→payments-db and gateway→payments-db.
  • menu-db ingress — only menu-svc may reach it on :5432. Closes gateway→menu-db.

Step 2 — The ingress policy on payments-svc (fixes Problem C)

Payments must only accept traffic from orders-svc. Every other source (gateway, menu, anything else) gets its SYN packet dropped at the payments pod's kernel.

payments-svc-ingress.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-svc-ingress-network-policy
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:                              # protect payments-svc
    matchLabels: { app: payments-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:                                 # ONLY orders-svc
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: orders-svc }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }

Step 3 — Effect on payments (orders ✓, gateway ✗, menu ✗)

The ingress gate on payments now compares every arriving packet's source label. Only app=orders-svc passes.

Step 4 — The three database ingress policies

Same pattern for every database — the only allowed source is that database's own service. Three tiny, near-identical policies together close Problems A and B.

orders-db-ingress.yamlYAML
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-db } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-svc } }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
payments-db-ingress.yamlYAML
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payments-db } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payments-svc } }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
menu-db-ingress.yamlYAML
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: menu-db } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: menu-svc } }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]

Step 5 — Effect on every database

Each DB now only opens for its paired service. Every direct-to-DB attempt from the gateway is dropped. Payments trying to reach orders-db is dropped.

Step 6 — What ingress fixed & what's still open

FlowBeforeAfter ingress
gateway → menu-db :5432works ⚠DENIED ✓
gateway → orders-db :5432works ⚠DENIED ✓
gateway → payments-db :5432works ⚠DENIED ✓
payments → orders-db :5432works ⚠DENIED ✓
gateway → payments :8080works ⚠DENIED ✓
menu → payments :8080works ⚠DENIED ✓
menu → payments-db :5432works ⚠DENIED ✓
— still open —
payments → evil.attacker.comworksstill works ⚠
gateway → arbitrary external URLworksstill works ⚠
orders → payments-db :5432 directworksstill works ⚠
Ingress only closes arrivals. A compromised payments-svc can still exfiltrate to the internet. A compromised orders can still open TCP :5432 directly to payments-db (bypassing the payments service). Egress policies (Case 3) close both.

Egress closes the windows

Ingress alone still lets a compromised pod try anything and reach the internet. Egress policies on the senders close the rest.

Case 3 — EGRESS policies on gateway, orders & payments
1 / 6

Step 1 — What ingress alone missed

After Case 2, arrivals are locked down. But a service can still initiate outbound traffic anywhere: gateway can call payments directly if the ingress gate ever weakens; payments can exfil to the internet; orders can talk to payments-db directly if the ingress gate weakens. Egress rules apply belt-and-suspenders — every call must pass the source's egress gate and the destination's ingress gate.

Reminder. Egress runs at the source pod's veth: "where am I allowed to reach?". Two gates for every packet.

Step 2 — The egress policy on api-gateway

The gateway should only reach menu and orders (plus DNS). It must never reach payments directly, and never reach any database.

api-gateway-egress.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: api-gateway-egress-network-policy, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:                                       # reach menu & orders only
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: menu-svc } }
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-svc } }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # NO payments-svc — gateway must not call payments
    # NO databases — gateway must not touch any DB
    - to:                                       # DNS
        - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
          podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } }
      ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]

Step 3 — Effect on the gateway

The gateway's own veth now filters outbound. Menu and orders : allowed. Payments : dropped at egress even before it reaches the payments ingress gate. Databases : dropped at egress. This is defense in depth — payments is now protected by both gates.

Step 4 — The egress policies on orders & payments

Same pattern. Orders can call payments (during checkout) and its own DB. Payments can only call its own DB. Neither can exfil to the internet or reach the wrong DB.

orders-svc-egress.yamlYAML
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-svc } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-db } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payments-svc } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # NO payments-db — orders must go through payments, never around it
    - to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } },
             podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]
payments-svc-egress.yamlYAML
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payments-svc } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payments-db } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    # NO orders-db — Problem B blocked at BOTH gates now
    # NO internet — payments cannot exfil
    - to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } },
             podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]

Step 5 — Effect on payments (belt and suspenders)

Payments can only reach payments-db. Two attempts fail — orders-db (Problem B, now blocked at both gates) and the external internet (exfil).

Step 6 — The full picture: every intended flow works, every misuse dropped

The mental model, complete. Ingress rules on payments and every database close Problem A, B, and C's arrivals. Egress rules on gateway, orders, and payments close the same problems at the source — giving defense in depth. A packet is only delivered when it passes both the sender's egress gate and the receiver's ingress gate. Every intended request goes through; every one of the seven attack paths is dropped.

One folder, three environments

Cluster jahez-dev · same folders, applied by the dev Argo CD app. Payment egress points at the provider’s sandbox range.

jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml (dev diff)YAML
    # [3] External payment provider — sandbox
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 198.51.100.0/24      # Mada sandbox — placeholder

VPC CNI runs in standard mode, so pods that start before their policy is compiled briefly allow all traffic.

Cluster jahez-staging · identical policies to prod; this is where every policy PR is tested with tests/verify.sh before merge.

Payment egress points at the provider’s test range. Hubble/flow logs are on, so every DROPPED flow is visible.

Cluster jahez-prod on EKS in me-central-1 · Argo CD syncs the folders after merge; nobody runs kubectl apply by hand.

VPC CNI runs with NETWORK_POLICY_ENFORCING_MODE=strict: a new pod starts with deny-all until its policies are compiled, so it is never briefly open.

Payments reaches orders-db (B)payments egress lists only payments-db; orders-db ingress lists only orderspayments-svc-network-policy

What you gain

What NetworkPolicy gives you

NetworkPolicy is the Kubernetes-native answer to microsegmentation — the idea that traffic should be allowed only between components that have a documented reason to talk. It is one of the foundational pillars of zero-trust networking inside the cluster.

🎯 Blast-radius reduction

A compromised pod can only reach what its policy allows. Lateral movement stops at the first deny.

🧾 Compliance

PCI-DSS 1.2/1.3, HIPAA, SOC 2 all require documented network segmentation. NetworkPolicy is the Kubernetes way to satisfy auditors.

🪪 Identity-based

Rules use pod labels — not IPs. Pods can move between nodes, scale up and down, get new IPs, and the policy keeps working.

🧪 Multi-tenancy

Namespace-scoped policies let you isolate teams, environments (prod vs. staging), or customer tenants on the same cluster.

📤 Egress control

Restrict which external endpoints pods can reach — block exfiltration to attacker-controlled domains, or limit cloud SDK access to specific buckets.

🔁 Declarative drift-free

Policies are GitOps-friendly. Apply via Argo/Flux; the CNI continuously reconciles kernel rules.

1.4 · Foundations

Comparisons

In one sentence

NetworkPolicy is the portable L3/L4 baseline every cluster gets; CNI-specific policies, a service mesh or AWS security groups add deny rules, hostnames, L7 or VPC-level control on top.

NetworkPolicy (v1)Cilium / Calico policy CRDsIstio AuthorizationPolicySecurity Groups for Pods (EKS)
LayerL3/L4 — IP, port, protocolL3/L4 + L7 (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka) + DNS namesL7 — HTTP method, path, headers, JWTL3/L4 at the ENI
Selects bypod + namespace labels, CIDRlabels, identities, FQDN, entities (host, world)service account identity (mTLS)security group IDs per pod
Deny rules / priority✕ allow-only, no order✓ deny + order (Calico tiers, Cilium deny)✓ ALLOW / DENY / CUSTOM✕ allow-only
Cluster-wide✕ namespaced✓ GlobalNetworkPolicy / CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy✓ root namespace✓ via SG
Egress to a hostname✕ CIDR only✓ toFQDNs / domain sets✓ via egress gateway✕
Encrypts / proves identity✕optional (WireGuard / IPsec)✓ mTLS✕
Portable✓ every conformant CNI✕ tied to that CNI✕ needs the mesh✕ AWS only
Who enforcesthe CNI on each nodethe CNI agent (eBPF)Envoy sidecar / ztunnelVPC (branch ENI)
Jahez usebaseline everywhere (this guide)not used — VPC CNI is the CNIfuture: L7 rules on paymentsRDS access from a few pods

When to choose something else

You need to allow a hostname

Payment providers rotate IPs behind api.provider.sa. v1 can only list CIDRs. Use Cilium toFQDNs / Calico domain sets, or route through an egress proxy and allow only the proxy.

You need deny or ordering

“Nobody may reach node metadata, whatever other policies say” needs priority. Use Calico tiers / Cilium deny, or the SIG Network AdminNetworkPolicy API where your CNI supports it.

You need L7 rules

“Only POST /charge from orders” needs HTTP awareness: an Istio AuthorizationPolicy or a Cilium L7 rule.

You need VPC resources

RDS or ElastiCache outside the cluster are protected by AWS security groups. Security Groups for Pods give chosen pods their own SG; NetworkPolicy still limits their egress.

2Architecture and workflows
2.1 · Architecture and workflows

Architecture

In one sentence

You write policies in git, the API server stores them, a controller resolves labels to pod IPs, and an agent on every node programs the kernel so each packet is checked at the pod’s own network interface.

Fig 2.1 — Where each part runs on the Jahez EKS cluster (me-central-1)

The parts

PartWhere it runsWhat it doesExample
Policy files① git repothe desired rules, one file per servicegit log --oneline -- jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
kubectl / Argo CD② your machine or CIsends the YAML to the API serverkubectl apply -f jahez-prod/
kube-apiserver③ control planevalidates the schema, RBAC and admission (Kyverno)kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f jahez-prod/
etcd③ control planestores the object; nothing is enforced yetkubectl get netpol -n jahez-prod
network-policy-controller③ control plane (EKS-managed)resolves selectors to pod IPs, writes PolicyEndpoint objectskubectl get policyendpoints -n jahez-prod
aws-eks-nodeagent④ every node (in aws-node)turns PolicyEndpoints into eBPF programs on pod vethskubectl logs -n kube-system ds/aws-node -c aws-eks-nodeagent
eBPF on the pod interface④ node kernelchecks every new connection; drops what is not allowedkubectl exec -n jahez-prod deploy/orders-svc-deployment -- nc -zv -w 3 payments-svc 8080

Where the object is stored

Where it lives

The object lives in etcd at the path /registry/networkpolicies/<namespace>/<name>. It is namespaced — a policy in jahez-prod only selects pods in jahez-prod. The kube-controller-manager does not act on it directly; instead, every node's CNI agent (e.g., Calico's calico-node, Cilium's cilium-agent) watches the API for NetworkPolicy events and translates them into local kernel rules.

Key insight. NetworkPolicy is enforced per-node, on the source side and the destination side. A rule allowing pod A → pod B requires both nodes (where A runs and where B runs) to agree. The CNI is responsible for keeping rules in sync as pods are scheduled and rescheduled.

CNI compatibility matrix

CNIv1 NetworkPolicyData planeL7 / extras
Calico✅iptables · eBPF · VPPGlobalNetworkPolicy, FQDN egress (Enterprise)
Cilium✅eBPF nativeL7 HTTP/Kafka/gRPC, FQDN egress, CiliumNetworkPolicy
Antrea✅Open vSwitchClusterNetworkPolicy with priority/deny
kube-router✅iptables + ipset—
Weave Net✅iptables—
Flannel❌ (alone)VXLAN routing onlyPair with Calico for policy
AWS VPC CNI✅ (since v1.14)eBPF (since 2023)Or pair with Calico
Azure CNI✅iptables / Cilium dataplane—
GKE Dataplane V2✅Cilium eBPFL7, FQDN with Anthos
Test before you trust. If you apply a policy and traffic still flows when it shouldn't — your CNI may not support NetworkPolicy. Verify with kubectl get pods -n kube-system and check your provider docs. AKS clusters created without --network-policy have zero enforcement.
Jahez EKS setting. Network policy is off in the VPC CNI by default. It is turned on with the add-on configuration {"enableNetworkPolicy": "true"}, which starts the aws-eks-nodeagent container in every aws-node pod.

NetworkPolicybaseline/11-allow-dns-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

Gives every pod back the one thing all of them need: DNS to kube-dns on UDP and TCP 53.

baseline/11-allow-dns-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Who is protected?  every pod in the namespace
  podSelector: {}
  # ② Which directions?  egress only
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  # ④ Where may it go?  kube-dns on UDP and TCP 53
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: ingress-nginx-egress-network-policy
  namespace: ingress-nginx
spec:

    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx }
  policyTypes: [Egress]

            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # DNS — even ingress-nginx needs it for upstream resolution
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

NetworkPolicyjahez-prod/20-api-gateway-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

The only pod reachable from ingress-nginx; it may call catalog, orders, users and cart.

jahez-prod/20-api-gateway-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-gateway-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # [1] Public traffic enters via ingress-nginx
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    # [2] Prometheus scrapes /metrics
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }
  egress:
    # [3] Routes to catalog-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [4] Routes to orders-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [5] Routes to users-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: users-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [6] Routes to cart-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: cart-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # Note: gateway does NOT call payments-svc directly — that's orders' job
    # Note: gateway does NOT call notify-svc — that's async via rabbitmq

NetworkPolicyjahez-prod/30-catalog-svc-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

Catalog accepts gateway, orders and cart, and talks only to catalog-db.

jahez-prod/30-catalog-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: catalog-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # Three internal callers — using matchExpressions for OR
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: app.kubernetes.io/name, operator: In,
                  values: [api-gateway, orders-svc, cart-svc] }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # Prometheus scrape
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # Only to the catalog MongoDB in jahez-data
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-db }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 27017 }]
    # DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

In one sentence

Orders accepts the gateway and calls catalog, payments, orders-db and rabbitmq.

jahez-prod/40-orders-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # [1] catalog-svc — line-item validation
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [2] payments-svc — charge the customer
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [3] orders-db (Postgres in jahez-data)
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    # [4] rabbitmq — publish OrderCreated event
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # [5] DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

NetworkPolicyjahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

Payments accepts only orders and calls payments-db, rabbitmq and the payment provider.

jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    jahez.sa/pci-scope: "true"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # Only orders-svc can call payments — gateway cannot
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # [1] payments-db (Postgres in jahez-data)
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-db }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    # [2] rabbitmq — publish PaymentSucceeded / PaymentFailed
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # [3] External payment provider — Mada / HyperPay
    # Get the actual CIDRs from your provider; these are illustrative
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 198.51.100.0/24
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]
    # [4] DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

NetworkPolicyjahez-prod/61-redis-rabbitmq-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

Redis accepts cart; RabbitMQ accepts orders, payments and notify.

jahez-prod/61-redis-rabbitmq-network-policy.yamlYAML
################################################################
# Redis — only cart-svc on 6379
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: redis-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: redis }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: cart-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 6379 }]
    # redis_exporter sidecar metrics, scraped by Prom
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9121 }]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---
################################################################
# RabbitMQ — accepts from orders, payments, notify; clusters on 25672
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: rabbitmq-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # AMQP producers/consumers
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: app.kubernetes.io/name, operator: In,
                  values: [orders-svc, payments-svc, notify-svc] }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # Cluster peering between rabbit pods (Erlang dist + epmd)
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 25672 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 4369 }
    # Prometheus scrape
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 15692 }]
  egress:
    # Cluster peer egress + DNS
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 25672 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 4369 }
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

NetworkPolicyjahez-prod/72-notify-svc-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

Notify accepts no app traffic; it consumes rabbitmq and calls SMS and S3.

jahez-prod/72-notify-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: notify-svc-network-policy, namespace: jahez-prod }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: notify-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # notify-svc is async — only Prom scrapes it
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # RabbitMQ — consume events
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # Unifonic SMS gateway
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 192.0.2.0/24
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]
    # S3 — invoices & receipts (broad egress with carve-outs)
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 198.18.0.0/24      # S3 me-central-1 — placeholder; use the com.amazonaws.me-central-1.s3 prefix list
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 198.18.1.0/24
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]
    # DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

NetworkPolicyjahez-data/60-databases-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

orders-db, users-db, payments-db and catalog-db each accept only their own service.

jahez-data/60-databases-network-policy.yamlYAML
################################################################
# orders-db (Postgres) — only orders-svc can connect
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-db-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    # Postgres exporter scraped by Prometheus
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9187 }]
    # Replica → primary streaming replication
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
  egress:
    # DNS only — Postgres needs no other egress
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    # Replica peer egress
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
---
################################################################
# users-db (Postgres) — only users-svc connects
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: users-db-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: users-db }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: users-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9187 }]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---
################################################################
# payments-db — only payments-svc connects (PCI in scope)
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-db-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
  annotations:
    jahez.sa/pci-scope: "true"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-db }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9187 }]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---
################################################################
# catalog-db (MongoDB) — catalog-svc only on 27017
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: catalog-db-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-db }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 27017 }]
    # Mongo replica set — peers
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-db
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 27017 }]
  egress:
    # Replica peer + DNS
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-db
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 27017 }]
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

NetworkPolicymonitoring/80-prometheus-network-policy.yaml
In one sentence

Prometheus may scrape every metrics port and call the API server for discovery.

monitoring/80-prometheus-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: prometheus-network-policy, namespace: monitoring }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # Grafana queries Prometheus
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: grafana }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # [1] scrape any workload pod in jahez-prod or jahez-data
    # — note: cross-NS, broad. Restrict ports to known scrape ports
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name, operator: In,
                  values: [jahez-prod, jahez-data, ingress-nginx] }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }   # app metrics
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9187 }   # postgres_exporter
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9121 }   # redis_exporter
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 15692 }  # rabbit prom plugin
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 10254 }  # nginx-ingress metrics
    # [2] DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    # [3] kube-apiserver — for service discovery
    # ipBlock sees the address AFTER kube-proxy DNAT, so list the real endpoints,
    # not the 10.96.0.1 Service VIP:  kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -n default
    - to:
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.12.34/32 }    # EKS control-plane ENI · me-central-1a
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.140.21/32 }   # EKS control-plane ENI · me-central-1b
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]

In one sentence

Grafana accepts only the internal VPN range and queries only Prometheus.

monitoring/81-grafana-network-policy.yamlYAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: grafana-network-policy, namespace: monitoring }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: grafana }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # Only employees on company VPN
    - from:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 10.50.0.0/16     # corp VPN range
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 3000 }]
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: loki }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 3100 }]
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

scripttests/verify.sh
In one sentence

Starts a probe pod in jahez-prod and checks that DNS works and everything else times out.

tests/verify.shbash
# Spin a debug pod inside jahez-prod
kubectl run debug -n jahez-prod --rm -it \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- bash

# Inside the pod — every check should fail (timeout) except DNS
nslookup kubernetes.default                 # ✓ works (DNS allowed)
curl -m 3 https://www.google.com            # ✗ timeout (no internet egress)
curl -m 3 http://orders-svc.jahez-prod      # ✗ timeout (no pod-to-pod yet)
curl -m 3 http://prometheus.monitoring:9090 # ✗ timeout (cross-NS denied)

💡 Command hint
run on your machine→print
    Deep dive →
    2.3 · Architecture and workflows

    How a packet is judged

    In one sentence

    Every new connection is checked twice: on the sender’s node against the sender’s egress rules, then on the receiver’s node against the receiver’s ingress rules — and both must allow it.

    Read each stage as Input → Logic → Output: what reaches the stage, the policy field that decides, and the verdict. The example is a real Jahez flow; the IPs are from the 1.2 inventory.

    One packet, orders-svc → payments-svc :8080 — Input → Logic → Output at each stage
    Whereorders-svc pod · node ip-10-50-31-200Blocksapp → kube-proxy / eBPF Service mapCommandkubectl exec -n jahez-prod deploy/orders-svc-deployment -- nc -zv -w 3 payments-svc 8080

    What happens. The orders app calls payments-svc:8080. DNS returns the Service VIP, and the node’s Service rules translate (DNAT) it to one payments pod IP before any policy is checked.

    ① INPUT
    CMD · what the app runs
    ⌨connect("payments-svc:8080")
    →
    ② LOGIC
    kube-proxy / Service
    payments-svc  ClusterIP 172.20.91.3:8080
  → endpoints 10.50.44.12:8080, 10.50.45.20:8080
    The Service VIP is replaced by a real pod IP.
    →
    ③ OUTPUT verdict
    📦TCP SYN 10.50.31.7 → 10.50.44.12:8080NEW
    1 packet · destination translated
    💡 Command hint
    start a shell in a pod→send a real packet→policy decides: allowed or dropped
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • exec run a command inside an existing container
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • jahez-prod namespace value
    • deploy/orders-svc-deployment a Deployment — kubectl picks one of its pods
    • -- everything after this goes to the command inside the container
    • nc network tool run inside the pod
    • -zv scan + verbose: report whether the TCP port opened (nc)
    • -w wait timeout in seconds (nc)
    • 3 port / number
    • 8080 port / number
    📌 Remember
    Policies never see 172.20.91.3. They see the pod IP — which is why ipBlock on a Service VIP never matches.
    ✕ When it fails
    If DNS is blocked (no TCP/UDP 53 egress), the app fails here with bad address 'payments-svc' before any packet leaves.
    1 / 6
    Wheresource node · orders pod veth (egress hook)Blockspolicy agent’s egress map for this podCommandkubectl get netpol -n jahez-prod

    What happens. The source node asks: does any policy select the orders pod with Egress in its policyTypes? If none does, egress is open and the packet skips to ③.

    ① INPUT
    PACKET · from the previous stage
    📦TCP SYN 10.50.31.7 → 10.50.44.12:8080
    POLICIES · selecting this pod
    📄default-deny-all-network-policypodSelector: {}
    📄allow-dns-network-policypodSelector: {}
    📄orders-svc-network-policyapp=orders-svc
    →
    ② LOGIC
    jahez-prod/40-orders-svc-network-policy.yaml
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
    Egress is listed, so the orders pod is egress-isolated.
    →
    ③ OUTPUT verdict
    🧱orders pod egressISOLATED
    3 policies select the pod · 3 list Egress
    💡 Command hint
    ask the API server / agent→print→nothing sent — cluster unchanged
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • get list objects from the API server
    • netpol short name for networkpolicy
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • jahez-prod namespace value
    📌 Remember
    One policy with Egress is enough to isolate; it does not matter which.
    ✕ When it fails
    If no policy listed Egress, the pod could reach anything — the classic “ingress-only” gap.
    2 / 6
    Wheresource node · orders pod vethBlocksunion of all egress rules for this podCommandkubectl describe netpol orders-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod

    What happens. The node merges the egress rules of all three policies and looks for one whose to peer matches the destination pod and whose ports match 8080/TCP.

    2.4 · Architecture and workflows

    Workflow — one apply traced

    In one sentence

    One kubectl apply travels from your file to the API server, into etcd, through a controller that turns labels into IPs, to an agent that programs every node — and only then are packets checked.

    The path of one apply — each step below lights only its own part
    How one apply travels — kubectl apply -f …/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    Whereyour machine / CI runnerBlockskubectlCommandkubectl apply -f jahez-network-policies/jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    • In prod, Argo CD runs the same apply after the PR is merged; in staging, the CI job does.
    • kubectl reads the file and finds one object: NetworkPolicy/payments-svc-network-policy in jahez-prod.
    • A wrong path fails here, before anything is sent.
    terminalbash

    • The agent on each node with a payments pod picks up the PolicyEndpoint.
    • It loads eBPF programs on the pod’s veth (ingress and egress hooks) and fills the allow maps.
    • Other CNIs use other primitives:
      • Calico (iptables mode) — programs Linux iptables chains and ipset sets per pod interface.
      • Calico (eBPF mode) / Cilium — loads eBPF programs attached to the pod's veth at tc ingress/egress, with a policy-map lookup per packet.
      • kube-router — uses ipsets + iptables.
      • Antrea — programs Open vSwitch flow rules.

    Part II

    Low Level

    Every field, every pattern and every command, in depth.

    3NetworkPolicy — object reference
    3.0 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    How a NetworkPolicy works

    In one sentence

    A NetworkPolicy answers four questions in order — who is protected, which directions it owns, who may come in, and where the pods may go — and the CNI turns those answers into allow-lists.

    ① The logic, read first

    A NetworkPolicy lives in one namespace and never changes the pods it selects; it only changes what their firewall allows. It lives until you delete it, and its rules apply to new connections within seconds of each change.

    Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
    ① Who is protected?podSelectorthe door the policy guards
    ② Which directions does it own?policyTypeswhich side of the door is locked
    ③ Who may come in?ingress[].from · ingress[].portsthe guest list at the front door
    ④ Where may it go?egress[].to · egress[].portsthe list of addresses it may visit
    API groupnetworking.k8s.io/v1
    Scopenamespaced
    Short namenetpol
    Status fieldnone
    Enforced bythe CNI
    Typical useone per service + baseline

    ② Full YAML — every field

    The real payments policy, with fields regrouped under the four questions and every field type used once.

    jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jahez-checkout
  annotations:
    jahez.sa/pci-scope: "true"
spec:
  # ① Who is protected?
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc
    matchExpressions:
      - { key: tier, operator: In, values: [backend] }
  # ② Which directions does this policy own?
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  # ③ Who may come in?
  ingress:
    - # ③a orders-svc pods in this namespace — API port only
      from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: http }        # named port → containerPort 8080
    - # ③b Prometheus in monitoring — namespace AND pod in one peer
      from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }
  # ④ Where may it go?
  egress:
    - # ④a payments-db in jahez-data
      to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-db }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
    - # ④b rabbitmq — AMQP and AMQPS as one port range
      to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5671, endPort: 5672 }
    - # ④c Mada gateway — placeholder CIDR with a carve-out
      to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
            except:
              - 203.0.113.128/25
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 443 }
    - # ④d DNS — UDP and TCP
      to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

    matchExpressionslistset-based rules; all must match (AND)
    Each item has key, operator and (for In/NotIn) values.
    Deep dive →
    •keystringrequiredthe label key

    Alone: every pod in matching namespaces. {} = every namespace. Use the built-in label kubernetes.io/metadata.name to pick one by name.
    Deep dive →

    Each key: value must be present on the namespace.
    Values
    { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }one label

    NotInvalue is not in the list, or the key is missing

    Cannot share an item with the selectors. Matches the address the node sees after Service DNAT, so it never matches a ClusterIP. Pod IPs are not meant to be selected by ipBlock.
