    ④ Deep dive — how rules combine

    The "rule" structure — AND vs OR

    This is where most people get tripped up. Within a single rule, the from peers are OR'd, the ports are OR'd, and the rule allows the cartesian product (from × ports). Multiple rules in the same ingress[] array are also OR'd.

    ⚡ AND inside a peer

    The exception that bites: when you put both podSelector AND namespaceSelector as keys of the same from/to entry (no dash before the second key), they are AND'd. Two separate dashed entries = OR; same entry, two keys = AND.

    OR — pods in either namespace OR with labelYAML
    from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { env: prod }
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels: { app: monitoring }
# allows: any pod in env=prod NS  OR
#         any pod with app=monitoring (in same NS)
    AND — only specific pods in specific NSYAML
    from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { env: prod }
    podSelector:
      matchLabels: { app: monitoring }
# allows: only pods with app=monitoring
#         that ALSO live in env=prod NS
    3.1 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    podSelector

    In one sentence

    podSelector picks the pods this policy protects, by label, from the policy’s own namespace; {} picks them all.

    Every NetworkPolicy starts by answering one question: which pods am I about to apply rules to? That is the job of spec.podSelector. Get this wrong and your policy applies to the wrong pods (or none at all).

    Three forms you will use daily

    1️⃣ Empty selector

    podSelector: {} — selects all pods in the namespace. Used for namespace-wide default-deny.

    2️⃣ matchLabels

    Equality match: pods that have all these labels. The 90% case.

    3️⃣ matchExpressions

    Set-based: In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist. Use when you need OR over label values or "has any version".

    podselector-examples.yamlYAML
    # A — Select all pods in the namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}

# B — Equality: pods labelled app=orders-svc AND tier=backend
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-svc
      tier: backend

# C — Set: pods labelled app IN (orders-svc, payments-svc)
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - { key: app, operator: In, values: [orders-svc, payments-svc] }

# D — Exists: any pod with a `version` label
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - { key: version, operator: Exists }

# E — Combined: equality AND set
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      tier: backend
    matchExpressions:
      - { key: env, operator: NotIn, values: [staging, test] }
    Always namespaced. spec.podSelector only selects pods in the policy's own namespace. There is no way for a NetworkPolicy in jahez-prod to select pods in monitoring. To restrict cross-namespace targeting use namespaceSelector in the peer side (covered in §10).

    Every combination in detail — with a real pod inventory

    The 5 examples above show the syntax. Now let's walk through every combination — one label, many labels, one expression, many expressions, both combined — and see exactly which pods each selector matches. We'll use the same pod inventory for all examples so you can watch the match set shrink and grow as the selector changes.

    📋 Pod inventory used in every example below
    Podapptierenvversioncanary
    orders-svc-0orders-svcbackendprodv2—
    orders-svc-1orders-svcbackendprodv2—
    payments-svc-0payments-svcbackendprodv1—
    payments-svc-canarypayments-svcbackendprodv2true
    catalog-svc-0catalog-svcbackendprod——
    api-gateway-0api-gatewayfrontendprodv3—
    orders-svc-stgorders-svcbackendstagingv2—
    test-runnertest-runner————

    All eight pods are in the same namespace. A dash means the label is absent, not empty.

    Part 1 · matchLabels only

    matchLabels does equality matching. Every key/value pair you list must match exactly. Multiple pairs are AND-ed — the pod must satisfy every one to be selected.

    Case 1.1 — One label

    The simplest case. Select every pod whose app label is orders-svc.

    case-1.1-one-matchlabel.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-svc
    PodSelected?Why
    orders-svc-0YESapp=orders-svc ✓
    orders-svc-1YESapp=orders-svc ✓
    orders-svc-stgYESapp=orders-svc ✓ (env=staging doesn't matter — not in selector)
    payments-svc-0noapp=payments-svc ≠ orders-svc
    catalog-svc-0noapp=catalog-svc ≠ orders-svc
    api-gateway-0noapp=api-gateway ≠ orders-svc
    test-runnernoapp=test-runner ≠ orders-svc
    Result: 3 pods. All three orders-svc pods, regardless of env. This is why environment separation via labels is important — and why running staging pods in the prod namespace is dangerous.

    Case 1.2 — Multiple labels (AND)

    Now narrow the selector with a second key. The pod must have both labels matching.

    case-1.2-multi-matchlabel.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:                # implicit AND between keys
      app: orders-svc
      env: prod
    PodSelected?Why
    orders-svc-0YESapp=orders-svc ✓ AND env=prod ✓
    orders-svc-1YESapp=orders-svc ✓ AND env=prod ✓
    orders-svc-stgnoapp matches, but env=staging ≠ prod → AND fails
    payments-svc-0noenv matches, but app fails
    all othersnoapp fails
    Result: 2 pods. The staging pod is now excluded. This is the 90% shape for production selectors — always pin env alongside app.

    Case 1.3 — Three labels (triple AND)

    You can chain as many as you need. Every additional pair narrows the match set further.

    case-1.3-three-matchlabels.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-svc
      env: prod
      version: v2            # pinning a specific version
    PodSelected?Why
    payments-svc-canaryYESapp ✓ AND env ✓ AND version=v2 ✓
    payments-svc-0noversion=v1 ≠ v2
    orders-svc-0noapp fails (even though version=v2 matches)

    Result: exactly one pod — the canary. Useful for canary-only policies (extra restrictive network rules for the canary while it's being validated).

    Part 2 · matchExpressions only

    matchExpressions uses set-based rules. Each expression has a key, an operator, and (for In/NotIn) a values list. There are four operators:

    OperatorMeaningNeeds values?
    InPod's label value is one of the listed values (OR inside the list)Yes
    NotInPod's label value is none of the listed values and the label existsYes
    ExistsPod has a label with this key (value doesn't matter)No — omit it
    DoesNotExistPod does not have a label with this keyNo — omit it

    Case 2.1 — One expression, In with one value

    Equivalent to matchLabels in effect, but the set-based form supports future expansion of the values list without rewriting.

    case-2.1-in-one-value.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: app
        operator: In
        values: [orders-svc]
    Same match set as Case 1.1 — 3 orders-svc pods. But now you can add another value to the list without changing structure.

    Case 2.2 — One expression, In with multiple values (OR)

    The values inside a single In are OR-ed. Pod matches if its label value is in any of the listed values. This is the killer feature of matchExpressions — matchLabels cannot express OR.

    case-2.2-in-multi-value.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: app
        operator: In
        values: [orders-svc, payments-svc, catalog-svc]  # OR
    PodSelected?Why
    orders-svc-0, -1, -stgYESapp=orders-svc is in the list ✓
    payments-svc-0, -canaryYESapp=payments-svc is in the list ✓
    catalog-svc-0YESapp=catalog-svc is in the list ✓
    api-gateway-0noapp=api-gateway not in the list
    test-runnernoapp=test-runner not in the list
    Result: 6 pods. Any pod matching any one of the three apps. This is how you write "select all backend services" without listing them individually across three separate NetworkPolicies.

    Case 2.3 — One expression, NotIn

    NotIn selects pods whose label value is none of the listed values. Critical gotcha: NotIn also requires the label to exist. A pod without the key at all is not selected by NotIn.

    case-2.3-notin.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: env
        operator: NotIn
        values: [staging, test]     # "select non-staging, non-test"
    PodSelected?Why
    orders-svc-0, -1YESenv=prod, not in [staging,test] ✓
    payments-svc-0, -canaryYESenv=prod ✓
    catalog-svc-0YESenv=prod ✓
    api-gateway-0YESenv=prod ✓
    orders-svc-stgnoenv=staging is in the list ✗
    test-runnerno ⚠env label absent → NotIn requires existence
    The NotIn trap. Notice test-runner — it has no env label at all. You might expect "not in staging/test" to select it, but Kubernetes' NotIn requires the key to exist. To catch label-less pods too, combine with DoesNotExist (Case 2.6).

    Case 2.4 — One expression, Exists

    Selects pods that have the given key, regardless of value. No values field.

    case-2.4-exists.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: version
        operator: Exists              # no values — key alone
    PodSelected?Why
    orders-svc-0, -1, -stgYEShas version=v2
    payments-svc-0YEShas version=v1
    payments-svc-canaryYEShas version=v2
    api-gateway-0YEShas version=v3
    catalog-svc-0nono version label
    test-runnernono version label

    Use case: enforce a policy on "every versioned workload" without listing versions.

    Case 2.5 — One expression, DoesNotExist

    The mirror of Exists. Selects pods that lack the given key.

    case-2.5-doesnotexist.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: canary
        operator: DoesNotExist
    Selects every pod except payments-svc-canary. Useful for "apply this policy to production traffic but exclude canaries" — flip a label to opt a pod out of a policy.

    Case 2.6 — Multiple expressions (AND between expressions)

    Multiple entries in matchExpressions are AND-ed. Pod must satisfy every expression to be selected. This is where the two-level logic kicks in: OR inside one In/NotIn, AND between expressions.

    case-2.6-multi-expressions.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - { key: app, operator: In, values: [orders-svc, payments-svc] }
      - { key: env, operator: In, values: [prod] }
      - { key: canary, operator: DoesNotExist }

    Reads as: (app is orders-svc or payments-svc) AND (env is prod) AND (no canary label).

    PodExpr 1
    app ∈ …    		Expr 2
    env = prod    		Expr 3
    no canary    		Selected?
    orders-svc-0✓✓✓YES
    orders-svc-1✓✓✓YES
    payments-svc-0✓✓✓YES
    payments-svc-canary✓✓✗no
    orders-svc-stg✓✗✓no
    catalog-svc-0✗✓✓no
    Result: 3 pods. All prod orders/payments pods except the canary. This is a real production shape — "apply the normal policy to stable production only; canary gets its own separate, stricter policy."

    Part 3 · Both matchLabels AND matchExpressions

    You can — and often should — combine both under one podSelector. When both are present, they too are AND-ed. Pod must satisfy every matchLabels pair and every matchExpressions rule.

    Case 3.1 — Simple combination

    Fix tier=backend with matchLabels (equality is more readable for equality), and use matchExpressions for the OR over apps.

    case-3.1-both-simple.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:                              # equality: use this style
      tier: backend
      env: prod
    matchExpressions:                         # set-based: use for OR / Exists
      - key: app
        operator: In
        values: [orders-svc, payments-svc]

    Reads as: tier=backend AND env=prod AND app ∈ {orders-svc, payments-svc}.

    Podtier=backendenv=prodapp ∈ …Selected?
    orders-svc-0✓✓✓YES
    orders-svc-1✓✓✓YES
    payments-svc-0✓✓✓YES
    payments-svc-canary✓✓✓YES
    orders-svc-stg✓✗✓no
    catalog-svc-0✓✓✗no
    api-gateway-0✗✓✗no

    Case 3.2 — Complex: matchLabels + multiple matchExpressions

    A realistic production selector combining all mechanisms:

    case-3.2-both-complex.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      tier: backend                       # equality
    matchExpressions:
      - { key: app, operator: In,
          values: [orders-svc, payments-svc, catalog-svc] }
      - { key: env,     operator: NotIn, values: [staging] }
      - { key: canary,  operator: DoesNotExist }
      - { key: version, operator: Exists }

    Reads as: tier=backend AND app ∈ {orders, payments, catalog} AND env ≠ staging (and env label exists) AND no canary label AND has a version label.

    Podtierappenv≠stgno canaryversion?Selected?
    orders-svc-0✓✓✓✓✓YES
    orders-svc-1✓✓✓✓✓YES
    payments-svc-0✓✓✓✓✓YES
    payments-svc-canary✓✓✓✗✓no
    catalog-svc-0✓✓✓✓✗no
    orders-svc-stg✓✓✗✓✓no
    api-gateway-0✗✗✓✓✓no
    Result: 3 pods. The three stable production backend services. Notice how each rule progressively filters the set — this is exactly the discipline a real production policy needs.

    The two-level logic rules — one table to remember

    All the cases above obey four simple rules. Memorise this table and you never need to guess:

    LevelCombinatorApplied to
    Between multiple keys in matchLabelsANDevery equality must hold
    Between multiple items in matchExpressionsANDevery expression must hold
    Between matchLabels and matchExpressionsANDboth blocks must hold
    Between values inside one In / NotInORthe label matches any listed value
    📎 Quick reference — which mechanism to use when
    • Need equality? → matchLabels (shorter, clearer)
    • Need OR (one label, several accepted values)? → matchExpressions with In
    • Need "has any value for this key"? → matchExpressions with Exists
    • Need "label absent"? → matchExpressions with DoesNotExist
    • Need "not one of these"? → matchExpressions with NotIn (remember: requires the key to exist)
    • Need OR between different keys (e.g. app=X or tier=Y)? → not possible in a single podSelector. Write two NetworkPolicies with the same rule set but different selectors.
    The critical non-feature. There is no OR between different keys within a single podSelector. If you truly need "app=orders OR tier=data", write two policies. Everything else is AND.

    Label hygiene matters

    NetworkPolicy is only as good as your label discipline. Adopt a consistent set of labels across every workload:

    📐 Recommended label schema
    • app.kubernetes.io/name — the application identifier (e.g. orders-svc)
    • app.kubernetes.io/component — role within the app (api, worker, db)
    • app.kubernetes.io/part-of — higher-level grouping (jahez-checkout)
    • tier — frontend / backend / data
    • env — prod / staging / dev
    3.2 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    policyTypes

    In one sentence

    policyTypes lists the directions the policy isolates; leave it out and Kubernetes guesses, often leaving egress open.

    If you remember one thing from this guide: always set policyTypes explicitly. Inferred behavior is the #1 source of "my policy isn't doing what I thought".

    What it does

    The policyTypes field tells Kubernetes which directions this policy is authoritative for. The presence of Ingress in the list means: "for the pods I select, this policy is locking down ingress; from now on only what I list under spec.ingress is allowed." Same for Egress.

    The three valid combinations

    A · [Ingress]

    Locks down ingress only. Egress remains default-allow (unless another policy locks egress).

    B · [Egress]

    Locks down egress only. Ingress remains default-allow.

    C · [Ingress, Egress]

    Locks down both directions in one policy.

    The inference rules (when policyTypes is omitted)

    If you do not set policyTypes, Kubernetes infers it from which of spec.ingress / spec.egress are present:
    • Has spec.ingress only → inferred as [Ingress]
    • Has spec.egress only → inferred as [Ingress, Egress] (yes, Ingress too — surprising!)
    • Has both → [Ingress, Egress]
    • Has neither → [Ingress]
    Never rely on inference. Always set policyTypes explicitly.

    The "block all egress" trick

    This is the canonical default-deny-egress policy. Note how the egress field is absent — that's not a typo:

    default-deny-egress.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}              # every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Egress]      # lock down egress
  # NOTE: no `egress:` key at all
  # → empty allow-list → ALL egress denied

    Compare this to a policy with egress: [] — same effect — versus one with egress: [{}] which means "one rule with no peers and no ports = allow all".

    3.3 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    Ingress rules

    In one sentence

    Each ingress rule allows its sources (from) on its ports, and all rules of all policies are added together.

    Ingress rules describe the allowed sources of traffic arriving at the selected pods. Each rule is a tuple of from peers and ports; if a packet's source matches at least one rule's from AND its destination port matches that same rule's ports, it is allowed.

    The shape of one rule

    ingress-rule-shape.yamlYAML
    ingress:
  - from:                        # list of NetworkPolicyPeer (OR'd)
      - podSelector: {...}
      - namespaceSelector: {...}
      - ipBlock: {...}
    ports:                       # list of NetworkPolicyPort (OR'd)
      - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
      - { protocol: TCP, port: 8443 }
  - from:                        # a SECOND rule, also OR'd with the first
      - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: monitoring } }
    ports:
      - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }

    Rule semantics — the four edge cases

    ShapeMeaning
    ingress: []Empty list — deny all ingress
    ingress: [{}]One rule with no from and no ports — allow all ingress
    ingress: [{ from: [...] }]From listed peers, on any port
    ingress: [{ ports: [...] }]From any source, but only on listed ports

    The four edge cases — walk through interactively

    The four shapes in the table above look like syntax minutiae, but each one produces a radically different runtime behavior. Walk through them on the same cluster from the previous sliders (user → gateway → orders-backend → orders-database + menu-svc). Each step shows the YAML, the resulting cluster diagram with from/port annotations, and the effective allow/deny for each source.

    Ingress edge cases · policy applied to orders-backend
    1 / 4

    Case A — ingress: [] — deny all ingress

    An empty list. There is an ingress key, but it has zero rules — so there is nothing to match against. Every incoming packet fails matching and is dropped.

    case-a-deny-all-ingress.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: case-a-network-policy, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress: []                              # empty list — no rule matches anything
    SourcePortResult
    api-gateway:8080DENIED
    menu-service:8080DENIED
    anyone elseanyDENIED

    Case B — ingress: [{}] — allow all ingress

    The list has one rule but that rule has no from and no ports. Absent from means "any source". Absent ports means "any port". The rule matches every packet.

    case-b-allow-all-ingress.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: case-b-network-policy, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - {}                                     # one rule, empty — matches EVERYTHING
    The subtle trap. Cases A and B look almost identical in YAML but produce opposite results. ingress: [] = deny all. ingress: [{}] = allow all. In production this has caused catastrophic outages on both sides — accidental total lockdown, or accidental total exposure.

    Case C — ingress: [{ from: [...] }] — sources listed, any port

    The from is set (specific source), but ports is absent. Only the listed sources can arrive, but they can hit any port the pod happens to expose — :8080, :9090, :22 if you left SSH open, everything.

    case-c-source-restricted-any-port.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: case-c-network-policy, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:                                # explicit source
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: api-gateway }
      # ports: omitted → gateway can hit ANY open port on backend
    SourcePortResult
    api-gateway:8080allowed
    api-gateway:9090allowed
    api-gateway:5005 (debug)allowed ⚠
    menu-serviceanyDENIED

    Case D — ingress: [{ ports: [...] }] — any source, only listed ports

    The mirror image of Case C. from is absent (any source), but ports is set. This is what you write for a public endpoint that anyone can hit, but only on the well-known port — like a health check that must survive despite the rest of the network being locked down.

    case-d-port-restricted-any-source.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: case-d-network-policy, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - # from: omitted → any source pod may connect
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    SourcePortResult
    api-gateway:8080allowed
    menu-service:8080allowed ⚠ (any source!)
    any random pod:8080allowed ⚠
    anyone:9090DENIED
    anyone:5005DENIED
    When to use Case D. Rarely for backends — you usually want from AND ports set. But useful for a public health endpoint that must be reachable from anywhere in the cluster (Kubernetes probes, load balancer health checks), or when your ingress controller has no fixed pod labels.

    Same four cases for egress

    Egress follows the exact same four shapes with the exact same semantics. The perspective flips: instead of "who is allowed to arrive at me", it's "where am I allowed to reach". Below, the policy is applied to api-gateway and controls what the gateway is allowed to call out to.

    Egress edge cases · policy applied to api-gateway
    1 / 4

    Case A — egress: [] — deny all egress

    Zero egress rules. Every outbound packet fails matching. The gateway can't even resolve DNS — it's totally sealed.

    egress-case-a.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: egress-a-network-policy, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: api-gateway }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress: []                              # empty — the gateway can reach NOTHING

    Case B — egress: [{}] — allow all egress

    One empty rule. No to and no ports means "any destination, any port". The gateway can reach everything — inside and outside the cluster. Basically default-allow, but with explicit acknowledgment in your manifest.

    egress-case-b.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: egress-b-network-policy, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: api-gateway }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - {}                                     # any destination, any port

    Case C — egress: [{ to: [...] }] — destinations listed, any port

    The gateway can reach the specified pods on any port. Useful when you want free-form ports between trusted pods but still restrict which pods.

    egress-case-c.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: orders-svc }
      # ports: omitted → gateway may reach backend on ANY port

    Case D — egress: [{ ports: [...] }] — any destination, only listed ports

    The gateway can reach any destination — but only on the listed ports. Useful when you want to enforce "only HTTPS out to the internet" without listing every partner CIDR.

    egress-case-d.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - # to: omitted → any destination pod OR external IP
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 443 }
    Real-world combination. A production gateway policy typically pairs Case C with Case D: rule 1 = specific pod + specific port (backend :8080), rule 2 = specific IP CIDR + port 443 (external providers), rule 3 = kube-dns :53. Union of the three = exactly what the gateway needs, nothing more.

    Worked example — orders-svc accepts only the gateway and the metrics scraper

    orders-ingress.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-ingress-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    # Rule 1 — API gateway can hit business endpoints
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: api-gateway }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    # Rule 2 — Prometheus from monitoring NS scrapes metrics
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }

    Named ports

    You can reference a port by its name rather than number — useful when the same policy targets pods that may use different numeric ports but standard names like http or metrics.

    named-port.yamlYAML
    ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: http           # resolved per-pod from containerPort name
    3.4 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    Egress rules

    In one sentence

    Each egress rule allows its destinations (to) on its ports; once egress is isolated, DNS must be allowed too.

    Egress rules are the symmetric counterpart of ingress: a list of allowed destinations. The mechanics are identical, but two real-world subtleties bite hard: DNS and stateful return traffic.

    DNS — the hidden dependency in every egress policy

    The classic break. You apply a default-deny-egress policy, then explicitly allow your app to reach Postgres on TCP/5432 — and the app still can't connect. Why? Because before any TCP connection, the app does getaddrinfo("postgres.databases.svc.cluster.local"), which is a UDP/53 query to kube-dns in kube-system. You blocked DNS. You always need to allow DNS in any egress-restricted pod.
    allow-dns.yaml — the snippet you will copy into every egress policyYAML
    egress:
  - to:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
        podSelector:
          matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
    ports:
      - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
      - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }    # for >512-byte responses / DoT

    Note we use kubernetes.io/metadata.name — a label automatically added to every namespace by the API server since v1.22, so we don't need to label kube-system ourselves.

    Stateful return — you do not need to allow it

    Common confusion: "I allowed egress to Postgres, do I need to allow ingress for the response?" — No. NetworkPolicy is conntrack-aware: the CNI tracks established connections, and reply packets in an allowed flow are automatically permitted. You only write rules for the connection initiation.

    Egress to external destinations

    Egress rules can target IP CIDR blocks for non-cluster destinations (a payment gateway, a SaaS API, the internet). See §10 for ipBlock mechanics, including the except field for fine-grained denies.

    egress-payment-gateway.yamlYAML
    egress:
  - to:
      - ipBlock:
          cidr: 203.0.113.0/24     # Mada / payment provider range
    ports:
      - { protocol: TCP, port: 443 }
    3.5 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    Ingress & egress — 3-tier example

    In one sentence

    A three-tier app secured end to end shows why every flow needs both the sender’s egress and the receiver’s ingress.

    The clearest way to internalize ingress and egress is to walk through a tiny but realistic three-tier app: a frontend, a backend API, and a database. We will start with zero policies (everything is open and the database is exposed), then progressively add policies until the frontend cannot reach the database — only the backend can — while every legitimate flow keeps working.

    9.5.1 Direction is always relative to the pod

    Before diagrams, the one fact that confuses everyone the first time: ingress and egress are always written from the perspective of the pod that the policy selects. If the pod is the database, "ingress" is traffic arriving at the database from someone else. If the pod is the backend, "egress" is traffic leaving the backend toward someone else. The same wire — backend → database — is the backend's egress and simultaneously the database's ingress.

    Fig 9.5.1 — A single connection is described from both ends. Both ends must permit it.
    Key consequence. When you debug a "blocked connection", you must check policies on both the source pod (egress) and the destination pod (ingress). Either side dropping = packet dies.

    9.5.2 The 3-tier app we'll secure

    A simple e-commerce frontend that calls a backend API, which reads/writes a Postgres database. All three live in the shop namespace.

    Fig 9.5.2 — The intended traffic: user → frontend → backend → database. The dangerous flow we want to prevent: frontend → database (skipping the backend).

    9.5.3 The Deployments (so the example is reproducible)

    three-tier-deployments.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels: { name: shop }
---
################ FRONTEND ################
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: frontend-deployment, namespace: shop }
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web, tier: frontend }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web, tier: frontend }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/shop-web:1.0
          ports: [{ containerPort: 80 }]
          env:
            - { name: BACKEND_URL, value: http://backend:8080 }
---
################ BACKEND ################
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: backend-deployment, namespace: shop }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api, tier: backend }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api, tier: backend }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/shop-api:1.0
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          env:
            - { name: DB_HOST, value: database }
            - { name: DB_PORT, value: "5432" }
---
################ DATABASE ################
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: database-deployment, namespace: shop }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: postgres, tier: data }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: postgres, tier: data }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          ports: [{ containerPort: 5432 }]
          env:
            - { name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD, value: change-me }

    9.5.4 BEFORE — no NetworkPolicy applied

    With zero NetworkPolicies, every pod can reach every other pod on every port. The frontend can connect directly to the database, completely bypassing the backend's authorization, validation, and audit logging.

    Fig 9.5.3 — BEFORE: an attacker who pops the frontend (XSS, SSRF, RCE in image upload) gets a direct line to Postgres. They can dump customers, modify orders, exfiltrate cards.

    Reproduce it from a frontend pod:

    verify-before.shbash
    # Exec into a frontend pod (no policy applied yet)
kubectl exec -n shop -it deploy/frontend-deployment -- sh

# From inside frontend, can you reach the database directly?
nc -zv database 5432
# Connection to database 5432 port [tcp/postgresql] succeeded! ⚠

nc -zv backend 8080
# Connection to backend 8080 port [tcp/*] succeeded! ✓ (intended)

    9.5.5 AFTER — with NetworkPolicies applied

    We are going to apply three NetworkPolicies. Together they enforce: frontend can talk to backend only; backend can talk to database only; database accepts only from backend; and nothing in the namespace can reach anything else.

    Fig 9.5.4 — AFTER: the same packet that worked in BEFORE now hits an iptables/eBPF DROP rule on the database pod's veth — silent timeout for the attacker.

    9.5.6 The three policies — with arrows annotated

    We'll write each policy and pair it with a small per-pod arrow diagram showing exactly what that policy lets in and out. Read these from the perspective of the selected pod.

    ① frontend-network-policy — selected pod is the frontend

    Fig 9.5.5 — frontend-network-policy: ingress from ingress-nginx; egress to backend only. Database egress is implicitly denied.
    01-frontend-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: frontend-network-policy
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:                                  # selects: the frontend
    matchLabels:
      tier: frontend
      app: web
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]            # lock down BOTH directions
  #  ┌─ INGRESS ──────────────────────────────────┐
  #  │ Allow public traffic from ingress-nginx    │
  #  │ on port 80 (the Service forwards to here). │
  #  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 80 }
  #  ┌─ EGRESS ───────────────────────────────────┐
  #  │ Allow ONLY two outbound flows:             │
  #  │  1. to the backend on port 8080            │
  #  │  2. to kube-dns for name resolution        │
  #  │ Everything else (incl. the database!)      │
  #  │ is implicitly denied.                       │
  #  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { tier: backend, app: api }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    - to:                                          # DNS — required for `getaddrinfo("backend")`
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

    ② backend-network-policy — selected pod is the backend

    Fig 9.5.6 — backend-network-policy: gatekeeper of the database. Only frontend in; only database out.
    02-backend-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: backend-network-policy
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:                                  # selects: the backend
    matchLabels:
      tier: backend
      app: api
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  #  ┌─ INGRESS ───────────────────────────────┐
  #  │ Accept ONLY from frontend on :8080.     │
  #  │ Anyone else (including a malicious      │
  #  │ workload in the same namespace) is      │
  #  │ silently dropped.                       │
  #  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { tier: frontend, app: web }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
  #  ┌─ EGRESS ────────────────────────────────┐
  #  │ Reach ONLY the database on :5432, plus  │
  #  │ DNS. The backend should not need        │
  #  │ internet egress at all in this example. │
  #  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { tier: data, app: postgres }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
    - to:                                          # DNS
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

    ③ database-network-policy — selected pod is the database (the most critical)

    Fig 9.5.7 — database-network-policy: even if a thousand other pods existed in the namespace, none of them could connect.
    03-database-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: database-network-policy
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:                                  # selects: the database
    matchLabels:
      tier: data
      app: postgres
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  #  ┌─ INGRESS ────────────────────────────────┐
  #  │ THE most important rule in the cluster:  │
  #  │ Postgres accepts ONLY from the backend.  │
  #  │ Even if frontend tries to connect to     │
  #  │ port 5432, the kernel drops the SYN.     │
  #  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { tier: backend, app: api }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
  #  ┌─ EGRESS ─────────────────────────────────┐
  #  │ Postgres has NO outbound business calls. │
  #  │ Only DNS for occasional name resolution. │
  #  │ A compromised DB cannot exfiltrate.       │
  #  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

    9.5.7 The two-sided handshake — why both policies matter

    For the frontend → database packet to be dropped, you only need one of the two policies to deny it. In our setup, both deny it — that's defense-in-depth:

    Fig 9.5.8 — Every cross-pod packet passes through both gates: source pod's egress policies AND destination pod's ingress policies. Both must allow.

    9.5.8 Verifying the lockdown

    Apply all three policies and re-run the probe. The same commands that worked BEFORE should now fail in exactly the right places.

    verify-after.shbash
    kubectl apply -f 01-frontend-network-policy.yaml
kubectl apply -f 02-backend-network-policy.yaml
kubectl apply -f 03-database-network-policy.yaml

###############################################
# Test 1 — frontend can still call backend ✓
###############################################
kubectl exec -n shop deploy/frontend-deployment -- \
  curl -m 3 -sf http://backend:8080/health
# expected: HTTP 200 OK

###############################################
# Test 2 — frontend CANNOT reach database ✗
###############################################
kubectl exec -n shop deploy/frontend-deployment -- \
  nc -zv -w 3 database 5432
# expected: timed out (the SYN is dropped at the kernel)

###############################################
# Test 3 — backend can reach database ✓
###############################################
kubectl exec -n shop deploy/backend-deployment -- \
  nc -zv -w 3 database 5432
# expected: succeeded

###############################################
# Test 4 — random debug pod cannot reach database ✗
###############################################
kubectl run probe -n shop --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  nc -zv -w 3 database 5432
# expected: timed out (no labels match database-network-policy.ingress)

    9.5.9 The summary table — same architecture, two universes

    FlowBEFORE (no policy)AFTER (3 policies)Why
    internet → frontend :80allowedallowedfrontend-network-policy.ingress permits ingress-nginx
    frontend → backend :8080allowedallowedfrontend.egress + backend.ingress both permit
    backend → database :5432allowedallowedbackend.egress + database.ingress both permit
    frontend → database :5432⚠ allowed (bad)deniedblocked at frontend.egress AND database.ingress
    database → internet⚠ alloweddenieddatabase.egress only allows DNS
    random pod → database⚠ alloweddenieddatabase.ingress only permits backend label
    frontend → some-other-namespace⚠ alloweddeniedfrontend.egress doesn't list cross-NS peers
    Mental model recap. Read every NetworkPolicy from the perspective of the pod its podSelector matches. ingress answers "who is allowed to arrive at me?" and egress answers "who am I allowed to reach out to?". Every cross-pod connection is governed by two policies — the source's egress and the destination's ingress — and either one denying drops the packet. Write both. Always.
    3.6 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    Peers

    In one sentence

    A peer names the other side of a connection — pods by label, namespaces by label, both together (AND), or an IP range.

    A "peer" is the entity on the other side of an allowed flow. Three kinds: podSelector, namespaceSelector, ipBlock. Every peer entry uses exactly one combination of these three keys.

    First — what from and to actually are

    Before diving into peer selectors, let's be precise about the two fields you write them under: ingress[].from and egress[].to. Both are lists of peer objects, and the exact rules are:

    from-to-anatomy.yaml — reading the structureYAML
    spec:
  ingress:
    - from:                            # ← a LIST of peers
        - podSelector: {...}          # peer 1 ─┐
        - namespaceSelector: {...}    # peer 2 ─┼─ OR-ed together
        - ipBlock: {...}              # peer 3 ─┘   (packet matches if ANY holds)
      ports: [...]                    # applied to whichever peer matched
    - from: [...]                     # ← a SECOND ingress rule (independent of the first)
      ports: [...]
  egress:
    - to:                              # same structure, opposite direction
        - podSelector: {...}
      ports: [...]

    Three logical layers you'll write against every day:

    LevelCombinatorMeaning
    Between multiple ingress: (or egress:) entriesORIndependent allow rules — packet passes if it matches any
    Between multiple peers in one from: (or to:) listORAny listed peer is an acceptable source/destination
    Between selector keys inside one peer (e.g. namespaceSelector + podSelector under the same dash)ANDBoth must hold — used for "specific pod in specific namespace"
    Between from/to and its sibling portsANDPacket must match a listed peer and a listed port
    Reading tip. Whenever you see a dash (-) in the peer list, ask yourself: "new peer or same peer?". New dash = new peer = OR. Same dash with more keys under it = one peer with multiple filters = AND. This one distinction generates 90% of NetworkPolicy bugs.

    The kube-system labelling requirement (silent DNS killer)

    Almost every non-trivial NetworkPolicy has an egress rule allowing pods to reach kube-dns. The standard shape looks like this:

    allow-dns-standard.yamlYAML
    egress:
  - to:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system   # ← this label
        podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
      - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
      - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

    This works only if the kube-system namespace actually has the label kubernetes.io/metadata.name=kube-system. Kubernetes ≥1.22 adds this label automatically via the NamespaceDefaultLabelName admission plugin — but three real-world scenarios make it disappear:

    🐛 Older cluster (<1.22)

    The auto-label never existed. Every NS created before you upgraded may lack it. Common in long-lived EKS/AKS/GKE clusters.

    🐛 GitOps / IaC drift

    A Terraform or Helm chart re-creates kube-system without the label; a controller strips it; a "clean up labels" job removed it. Silent.

    🐛 kube-dns pod not labelled k8s-app

    CoreDNS versions differ — some use k8s-app: kube-dns, some use app.kubernetes.io/name: coredns. Your policy targets the wrong label and matches nothing.

    The failure mode is diabolical: DNS silently stops working for every pod under the policy. Applications hang on getaddrinfo, time out after 30 seconds, log opaque "connection refused" errors, and the cluster looks fine — Prometheus, ingress controller, everything else healthy. You'll spend hours chasing a "DNS problem" that's actually a missing label.

    Verify and fix — the 3 commands you should always run

    verify-dns-labels.shbash
    # 1. Does the kube-system namespace have the expected label?
kubectl get ns kube-system --show-labels
# Expect to see: kubernetes.io/metadata.name=kube-system

# 2. What labels does the DNS pod carry?
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
# If empty, try the CoreDNS variant:
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=coredns

# 3. If missing, add both labels explicitly (idempotent, safe to re-run)
kubectl label ns kube-system kubernetes.io/metadata.name=kube-system --overwrite
# For the pod label, patch the CoreDNS Deployment's pod template if needed
    Defensive pattern. Instead of assuming one label works, write the DNS egress rule as two peers (OR) — covering both label conventions. If k8s-app: kube-dns matches nothing, app.kubernetes.io/name: coredns catches it:
    allow-dns-defensive.yaml — belt and suspendersYAML
    egress:
  - to:
      # peer 1: classic k8s-app label
      - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
        podSelector:       { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } }
      # peer 2: modern CoreDNS label
      - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
        podSelector:       { matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: coredns } }
    ports:
      - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
      - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    The label-vs-name confusion. kubernetes.io/metadata.name is the label. It's not the namespace name itself — it's a label whose value happens to be the namespace name. NetworkPolicy has no way to target a namespace by name directly; you must always go through labels. Every namespace you want to target from any NetworkPolicy needs a stable, unique label.

    Best-practice labelling for your own namespaces

    Take the same discipline to your own namespaces. Never rely on the auto-injected label alone — add a purpose-specific one:

    namespace-labels.yaml — canonical setYAML
    apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: jahez-prod
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod       # auto-added ≥1.22, add explicitly anyway
    purpose: application                        # or: platform / data / monitoring
    env: prod                                    # prod / staging / dev
    team: payments                                # owning team
    pci-scope: "true"                              # for PCI-relevant NS only

    Now you can write NetworkPolicies against any of these labels — "allow ingress from any prod namespace" or "allow egress only to non-PCI namespaces" — without ever hard-coding a namespace name.

    The three peer types

    🟦 podSelector

    Pods in the policy's own namespace matching the given labels.

    Cross-namespace? Combine with namespaceSelector.

    🟪 namespaceSelector

    All pods in namespaces matching the given labels (including the policy's own NS, if labelled).

    🟧 ipBlock

    External CIDR. Used for traffic from/to outside the cluster (or to clamp pod-to-pod by IP).

    Five peer patterns you will write

    peer-patterns.yamlYAML
    # 1. Pods in the same namespace
- podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: api-gateway }

# 2. All pods in another namespace (use NS auto-label)
- namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }

# 3. Specific pods in another namespace (AND — same dash entry!)
- namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }

# 4. External CIDR (the internet, a VPC subnet, a third-party API)
- ipBlock:
    cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
    except:
      - 10.0.0.0/8           # carve out internal RFC1918
      - 169.254.169.254/32  # cloud metadata service!

# 5. Allow from any pod in any namespace (use sparingly)
- namespaceSelector: {}    # {} = all namespaces
    The metadata-service trap. On AWS / GCP / Azure, pods can hit 169.254.169.254 to grab the node's IAM credentials. Always add this IP to except in any wide-open egress allow list, or use IRSA / Workload Identity / Pod Identity which bypasses IMDS entirely.

    The cluster-mesh diagram — one rule, three peers, both directions

    Fig 10.1 — One pod, three peer types: podSelector (intra-NS), ns+pod (cross-NS), ipBlock (external)

    All AND / OR combinations for peers — walk through interactively

    The "five peer patterns" above show the shapes. Now let's step through every AND/OR combination with a concrete cluster, so the layered logic becomes muscle memory. All examples use the same setup:

    📋 Cluster setup for the sliders below
    • jahez-prod — namespace holding the app (label purpose=application, env=prod)
    • monitoring — Prometheus namespace (label purpose=monitoring)
    • ci — CI runners namespace (label purpose=ci)
    • data — shared databases (label purpose=data)
    • External Mada payment API at 203.0.113.0/24
    • Policy target: orders-svc in jahez-prod
    OR vs AND — the peer-level distinction that trips everyone
    1 / 7

    Step 1 — The one rule that matters

    In a from: or to: list, each dash (-) starts a new peer. Multiple peers = OR. Multiple selectors inside one peer entry = AND.

    Step 2 — OR at the peer level (multiple dashes)

    Allow orders-svc to accept traffic from api-gateway OR from cart-svc — both in the same namespace. Two separate dash entries. The pod matches if it's either.

    or-pattern.yamlYAML
    spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-svc } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } }   # peer 1
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: cart-svc } }      # peer 2
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]

    Step 3 — OR at peer level, mixing pod & namespace selectors

    Peers in the same list can be of different types. Allow orders-svc to accept from api-gateway pods OR any pod in the monitoring namespace.

    or-mixed-types.yamlYAML
    ingress:
  - from:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels: { app: api-gateway }         # peer 1: same-NS pod
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }  # peer 2: whole NS
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    Reads as: source is (api-gateway in jahez-prod) OR (any pod in monitoring NS). Two peers of different types, OR-ed.

    Step 4 — AND inside one peer (the cross-NS specific pattern)

    To allow only prometheus in monitoring — not every pod in monitoring — put both selectors under the same dash. Now the peer means "namespace matches monitoring AND pod matches app=prometheus".

    and-inside-one-peer.yamlYAML
    ingress:
  - from:
      - namespaceSelector:                        # ┐  same dash
          matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
        podSelector:                              # ┘  = AND
          matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]

    Step 5 — The trap: what looks like AND but is actually OR

    Beginners often type this expecting AND, and get a much wider allow-list than intended:

    trap-looks-and-is-or.yaml — WRONG for "prometheus in monitoring only"YAML
    ingress:
  - from:
      - namespaceSelector:                        # dash 1 → peer 1
          matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
      - podSelector:                              # dash 2 → peer 2 (independent!)
          matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]

    Two dashes = two peers = OR. This actually means: allow from (any pod in monitoring NS) OR (any pod anywhere with app.kubernetes.io/name=prometheus) — including a rogue prometheus in some other namespace. To get "prometheus in monitoring only" you must put both selectors under a single dash (Step 4).

    The visual test. Count the dashes. Two dashes at the same indentation level = two peers = OR. If you want AND, there is exactly one dash, and the additional selectors line up underneath it at the deeper indent.

    Step 6 — Mixed: some peers OR'd, one uses AND internally

    Combine both. Peer 1 uses AND internally (prometheus in monitoring), peer 2 is a same-NS pod, peer 3 is an ipBlock. The three peers are OR-ed.

    mixed-peers.yamlYAML
    ingress:
  - from:
      # Peer 1 — internal AND: prometheus AND monitoring NS
      - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring } }
        podSelector:       { matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus } }
      # Peer 2 — simple same-NS pod
      - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } }
      # Peer 3 — external CIDR
      - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.0.0/16 }
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]

    Reads as: (prometheus in monitoring) OR (api-gateway in same NS) OR (any IP in 10.50/16). Three peers, three sources of truth, unioned.

    Step 7 — Effective-set truth table for Steps 2–6

    SourceStep 2
    OR pods    		Step 3
    OR mixed    		Step 4
    AND cross-NS    		Step 5
    trap (OR)    		Step 6
    mixed
    api-gateway (jahez-prod)✓✓✗✗✓
    cart-svc (jahez-prod)✓✗✗✗✗
    menu-svc (jahez-prod)✗✗✗✗✗
    prometheus (monitoring)✗✓✓✓✓
    grafana (monitoring)✗✓✗✓ ⚠✗
    rogue prometheus (elsewhere)✗✗✗✓ ⚠✗
    10.50.1.20 (corp VPN)✗✗✗✗✓
    172.16.0.10 (other CIDR)✗✗✗✗✗

    Notice the ⚠ column for Step 5 — the trap admits grafana and any rogue prometheus in any namespace. Step 4 (real AND) admits only prometheus in monitoring.

    Every peer-type combination — one entry at a time
    1 / 7

    Step 1 — podSelector only (same-NS pods)

    peer-pod-only.yamlYAML
    from:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels: { app: api-gateway }

    Matches pods in the same namespace as the policy labelled app=api-gateway. Cannot reach across namespaces on its own.

    Step 2 — namespaceSelector only (all pods in matching NS)

    peer-ns-only.yamlYAML
    from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }

    Matches every pod in every namespace whose labels match. If two namespaces carry the same label, both match. Includes the policy's own NS if it happens to carry the label.

    Step 3 — namespaceSelector + podSelector (AND, cross-NS)

    peer-ns-and-pod.yamlYAML
    from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
    podSelector:
      matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }

    The most-used cross-namespace shape: specific pod in specific namespace. Both must hold. This is how you allow prometheus but not grafana from monitoring.

    Step 4 — ipBlock only (external CIDR)

    peer-ipblock.yamlYAML
    to:
  - ipBlock:
      cidr: 203.0.113.0/24       # Mada gateway — placeholder; use the provider’s published CIDRs

    Matches any IP inside the CIDR. Used for external providers (payment APIs, SaaS, SMS gateway, S3, corp VPN range). Cannot be combined with pod or namespace selectors in the same peer — ipBlock is standalone.

    Step 5 — ipBlock with except

    peer-ipblock-except.yamlYAML
    to:
  - ipBlock:
      cidr: 0.0.0.0/0              # the entire internet
      except:
        - 10.0.0.0/8                # private RFC1918 — never egress here
        - 169.254.169.254/32       # cloud metadata service (IMDS) — ALWAYS carve out
        - 100.64.0.0/10             # cloud CGNAT range
    Never forget 169.254.169.254. That's the cloud metadata service. A pod that can reach it can steal the node's IAM credentials on AWS/GCP/Azure. Every wide-open ipBlock must except it — or better, use IRSA / Workload Identity / Pod Identity to remove the reason to hit it in the first place.

    Step 6 — All three peer types in one from list (OR)

    peer-all-three.yamlYAML
    ingress:
  - from:
      - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } }             # same-NS pod
      - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring } }
        podSelector:      { matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus } }
      - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.0.0/16 }                                # corp VPN
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]

    Three peers, three different types, all OR-ed. This is the most common production shape for a service with internal callers, cross-NS metrics scraping, and corp-VPN admin access.

    Step 7 — The definitive reference table

    Peer shapeSame NSCross-NS?External IP?Typical use
    podSelectoryesnonoNeighbor service in the same NS
    namespaceSelectorif labelledyesnoAny pod in some other NS
    namespaceSelector + podSelectorif labelledyesnoSpecific pod in specific NS ← most-used cross-NS pattern
    ipBlock——yesExternal provider, VPN, cloud CIDR
    ipBlock + except——yesBroad allow with carve-outs (IMDS, RFC1918)
    — across the list —
    Multiple peers in one from/toAll OR-ed. Any listed peer is acceptable.
    Multiple selector keys inside one peerAND-ed. All must hold. Use for "pod X in NS Y".
    ipBlock combined with pod/ns selectorsIllegal. ipBlock is standalone. Kubernetes rejects the manifest.
    ipBlock sees the pod IP, never the Service VIP. The node translates a Service ClusterIP to a pod IP before the policy check. An ipBlock of 10.96.0.1/32 (the API Service) never matches; list the endpoint IPs from kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -n default instead. See 4.6.
    3.7 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    Ports

    In one sentence

    A port item narrows a rule to one protocol and a port number, a named container port, or a range; leaving ports out allows them all.

    ① The logic, read first

    FormYAMLMatchesWatch out
    No portsports: absentevery port, every protocoloften wider than intended
    Number{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }that one portprotocol defaults to TCP — DNS needs UDP and TCP
    Named port{ port: http }the containerPort named http on the destination podin egress, the name is looked up on the destination pods; different pods may map it to different numbers
    Range{ port: 7000, endPort: 7010 }every port 7000…7010port must be a number; stable since 1.25
    Protocol only{ protocol: UDP }every UDP portuseful for “all UDP to kube-dns” but rarely needed

    ② Full YAML

    jahez-prod/payments-ports-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: payments-svc-pod
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc
spec:
  containers:
    - name: payments
      image: ghcr.io/jahez/payments-svc:2.8.0
      ports:
        - { name: http, containerPort: 8080 }      # ← the name a policy can use
        - { name: metrics, containerPort: 9090 }
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-ports-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Who is protected?
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
  # ② Which directions?
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  # ③ Who may come in — and on which ports?
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP          # TCP | UDP | SCTP  (default TCP)
          port: http             # named port → 8080 on THIS pod
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 9090             # a number
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 7000             # range 7000–7010 (cluster gossip)
          endPort: 7010
    ⌘ Commands for this file
    kubectl apply -f jahez-prod/payments-ports-network-policy.yaml

    check which names the pod defines

    protocolstringTCP, UDP or SCTP

    3.8 · NetworkPolicy — object reference

    What Kubernetes writes

    In one sentence

    Kubernetes adds only bookkeeping to a NetworkPolicy — there is no status — so to see what is really enforced you read what the CNI wrote.

    You write

    metadata.name, namespace, labels, annotations, and the whole spec.

    Kubernetes / the CNI writes

    uid, generation, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp, managedFields, the last-applied annotation — and, on EKS, one PolicyEndpoint per policy.

    kubectl get netpol payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod -o yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  annotations:
    jahez.sa/pci-scope: "true"
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |     # written by kubectl apply
      {"apiVersion":"networking.k8s.io/v1","kind":"NetworkPolicy",...}
  creationTimestamp: "2026-11-19T21:40:12Z"      # written by the API server
  generation: 3                                   # +1 on every spec change
  managedFields:                                  # who owns which field
    - manager: argocd-controller
      operation: Apply
  name: payments-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
  resourceVersion: "48211907"                     # changes on every write
  uid: 3f1c2a9e-7b44-4d8e-9a51-0c6e2d7f8b10
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  # … your rules, unchanged …
    No status, no events. A policy whose selector matches zero pods, or a CNI that ignores policies, looks exactly the same as a working one. kubectl describe shows no warnings. Always test with a probe (5.3).
    kubectl get policyendpoints -n jahez-prod -o yaml (one item)YAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.aws/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyEndpoint                               # written by the EKS controller
metadata:
  name: payments-svc-network-policy-x7k2p
  namespace: jahez-prod
  ownerReferences:
    - kind: NetworkPolicy
      name: payments-svc-network-policy
spec:
  policyRef: { name: payments-svc-network-policy, namespace: jahez-prod }
  podSelectorEndpoints:                            # the protected pods, as IPs
    - { podIP: 10.50.44.12, name: payments-svc-deployment-84f6d7c5b-t3v6x, hostIP: 10.50.44.115 }
    - { podIP: 10.50.45.20, name: payments-svc-deployment-84f6d7c5b-w8p1c, hostIP: 10.50.45.18 }
  ingress:
    - { cidr: 10.50.31.7, ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }] }   # orders pod
    - { cidr: 10.50.46.3, ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }] }   # orders pod
  egress:
    - { cidr: 203.0.113.0/24, except: [203.0.113.128/25], ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }] }

    4Patterns
    4.1 · Patterns

    Default-deny baseline

    In one sentence

    Select every pod with podSelector: {}, list both policyTypes, and add no rules: the namespace now allows nothing until you add it back.

    The single most important pattern in this entire guide. Every namespace that holds workloads should ship with a default-deny policy applied first, before any allow-specific rules. This flips the namespace from "allow by default" to "deny by default", and is the cornerstone of zero-trust microsegmentation.

    Three flavors

    A · deny ingress only

    Pods can still call out (DNS works, calls to APIs work). Nothing can reach in unless a later policy allows it.

    B · deny egress only

    Pods accept traffic, but cannot reach anything — not even DNS. Use only with a paired allow-DNS policy.

    C · deny both

    Total isolation. The strongest baseline. Combine with explicit allow-DNS + allow-business policies.

    The canonical default-deny-all

    00-default-deny-all.yaml — apply first to every namespaceYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}                # every pod in this namespace
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
  # no `ingress:` and no `egress:` keys
  # → empty allow-list in both directions
  # → every pod here flips to default-deny in BOTH directions

    This single 11-line YAML is the most powerful security control in the cluster. From the moment it's applied, no pod in jahez-prod can talk to anything — not the API server, not DNS, not Postgres, not the internet. Your apps will start failing immediately. That is the point.

    The companion: allow-DNS

    Always pair the default-deny with an allow-DNS policy. Without DNS, almost nothing works (image pulls happen at the kubelet level so they're unaffected, but every http.Get("https://api.example.com") in your app fails).

    01-allow-dns.yaml — companion to default-denyYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    Order doesn't matter. Because policies are unioned, you can apply allow-dns before default-deny-all or after — the resulting allow-list is identical. Apply both together via Kustomize/Helm to keep them in lockstep.
    4.2 · Patterns

    Allow-specific (workhorse)

    In one sentence

    One policy per service, holding its ingress callers and egress dependencies, is the workhorse you will write most.

    After default-deny, every meaningful flow needs an explicit allow. The allow-specific pattern is one policy per service that lists the exact upstream and downstream pods it talks to.

    The three-rule template

    For any backend service, you typically need three rule blocks:

    1. Ingress from upstream callers — the gateway, other internal services that depend on you.
    2. Egress to downstream dependencies — your database, the cache, the next microservice.
    3. Egress to platform services — DNS (always), metrics push (if used), logging sidecar.
    orders-svc-allow.yaml — the workhorse templateYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-svc-allow-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # [1] from API gateway only
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    # [2] from monitoring NS — Prometheus scrape
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }
  egress:
    # [3] to orders-db (Postgres) in the data NS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
    # [4] to catalog-svc for product lookups
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    # [5] to payments-svc for charging
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    # [6] DNS — required for every named lookup above
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

    Notice every rule is precise: a specific source/destination, a specific port. No wildcards. This is what zero-trust looks like in a Kubernetes manifest.

    4.3 · Patterns

    Cross-namespace allow

    In one sentence

    Cross-namespace traffic needs a namespaceSelector on both sides: the sender’s egress names the target namespace and the receiver’s ingress names the source.

    When the source pod is in namespace A and the target is in namespace B, you have to be precise on both ends — the policy in B must allow A's pods, and (if A has egress restrictions) the policy in A must allow B's pods.

    Two namespaces, mutual policies

    Fig 13.1 — Both sides must agree: orders-svc egress allows DB; orders-db ingress allows orders-svc
    Use the auto-label. Since Kubernetes 1.22, every namespace gets the label kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<ns-name> automatically. Use it as your default namespaceSelector match — no manual labelling needed.

    Policy on the target side (jahez-data)

    orders-db-allow.yaml — in jahez-data namespaceYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-db-allow-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
    4.4 · Patterns

    DNS egress

    In one sentence

    Every egress-isolated pod needs DNS: allow kube-dns in kube-system on UDP and TCP 53.

    DNS deserves its own pattern section because it breaks more egress policies than every other rule combined. The mechanics are subtle.

    The DNS resolution path inside a pod

    Fig 14.1 — Every named lookup goes UDP/53 → kube-dns in kube-system before any TCP can flow

    The cluster-wide allow-DNS

    Apply this in every namespace that has an egress-restricted policy. It is one of the few policies you can safely treat as a "boilerplate copy".

    allow-dns-everywhere.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod     # repeat per namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}                 # every pod
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

    FQDN-based egress: the L7 frontier

    Vanilla NetworkPolicy is L3/L4 only — it cannot match on hostnames. If you want to allow egress to api.stripe.com without pinning to fragile CIDRs, you need:

    • CiliumNetworkPolicy with toFQDNs
    • Calico Enterprise with DNS-policy
    • Service mesh (Istio Egress Gateway) sitting in front

    For the project below we'll stick to native v1 NetworkPolicy and use ipBlock for the payment provider — but know that L7 is where you go when CIDRs become unmaintainable.

    4.5 · Patterns

    External CIDR egress

    In one sentence

    Traffic leaving the cluster can only be matched by IP range: list the provider’s CIDRs, or allow 0.0.0.0/0 with carve-outs for metadata and private ranges.

    When a pod must reach something outside the cluster — a SaaS API, a payment processor, an on-prem database, the public internet — you allow the destination via ipBlock. Two patterns dominate: precise allow-list and wide-open with carve-outs.

    Pattern A — precise allow-list (preferred)

    payments-egress-precise.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-egress-external-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    # Mada / payment processor — get the CIDR from the provider
    - to:
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 203.0.113.0/24 }
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 198.51.100.0/24 }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 443 }

    Pattern B — open internet with carve-outs

    For a service that legitimately needs broad internet egress (image-processing pulling random URLs, analytics fan-out), use 0.0.0.0/0 with except to still block the cluster-internal RFC1918 ranges and the dangerous metadata service IP.

    internet-egress-with-carveouts.yamlYAML
    spec:
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except:
              - 10.0.0.0/8            # internal cluster overlay
              - 172.16.0.0/12         # internal RFC1918
              - 192.168.0.0/16        # internal RFC1918
              - 169.254.169.254/32    # cloud metadata service !!
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 443 }
    Always except 169.254.169.254/32. This is the IMDS — Instance Metadata Service — on EC2, GCE, Azure. From inside a pod it returns the node's IAM credentials. SSRF + open egress = full cloud account compromise. Use IRSA (EKS), Workload Identity (GKE), or AAD Pod Identity (AKS) to give pods their own scoped identity, and block IMDS unconditionally.

    The except field — gotchas

    ⚠️ except CIDRs must be subsets of cidr

    If your cidr is 10.0.0.0/16 you cannot except: 192.168.0.0/24 — the API server rejects it. The exceptions must fall within the parent block.

    ⚠️ except is per-ipBlock, not global

    If you have two ipBlock entries, each has its own except. They do not interact.

    The CIDRs in this guide are placeholders from the documentation ranges (203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 192.0.2.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15). Get the real ranges from each provider, and for S3 from the com.amazonaws.me-central-1.s3 managed prefix list.
    4.6 · Patterns

    Monitoring & API server

    In one sentence

    Monitoring needs the widest legal reach: egress to every metrics port in the app namespaces, plus the API server — listed by its real endpoint IPs, never its Service VIP.

    monitoring/prometheus-scrape-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: prometheus-scrape-network-policy
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  # ① Who is protected?
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
  # ② Which directions?
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  # ④ Where may it go?
  egress:
    - # ④a scrape every pod's metrics port in the app namespaces
      to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name, operator: In, values: [jahez-prod, jahez-data] }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9187 }      # postgres-exporter
    - # ④b Kubernetes API for service discovery
      # ipBlock sees the address AFTER DNAT — list the real endpoints,
      # not the 10.96.0.1 / 172.20.0.1 Service VIP:
      #   kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -n default
      to:
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.12.34/32 }    # EKS control-plane ENI · me-central-1a
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.140.21/32 }   # EKS control-plane ENI · me-central-1b
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 443 }
    - # ④c DNS
      to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    ⌘ Commands for this file
    kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -n default
    find the real API server IPs to put in ipBlock
    💡 Command hint
    ask the API server / agent→print→nothing sent — cluster unchanged
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • get list objects from the API server
    • endpoints the Endpoints object — the real pod / node IPs behind a Service
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • default namespace value
    kubectl apply -f monitoring/prometheus-scrape-network-policy.yaml
    apply it
    💡 Command hint
    read the file→API server validates→store in etcd→CNI programs every node
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • apply create the object, or update it if it exists (server keeps a merge record)
    • -f file, folder or URL to read manifests from
    • monitoring/prometheus-scrape-network-policy.yaml the manifest file or folder
    kubectl exec -n monitoring deploy/prometheus-deployment -- wget -qO- -T 3 https://kubernetes.default.svc/healthz
    prove the API is reachable
    💡 Command hint
    start a shell in a pod→send a real packet→policy decides: allowed or dropped
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • exec run a command inside an existing container
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • monitoring namespace value
    • deploy/prometheus-deployment a Deployment — kubectl picks one of its pods
    • -- everything after this goes to the command inside the container
    • wget network tool run inside the pod
    • 3 port / number
    • https://kubernetes.default.svc/healthz URL to call
    kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -n default example outputstdout
    NAME         ENDPOINTS                           AGE
kubernetes   10.50.12.34:443,10.50.140.21:443   412d
    EKS control-plane IPs can change during upgrades. Re-run the endpoints command after every cluster upgrade, or allow the whole VPC subnet the control-plane ENIs live in.

    5.0 · Commands

    How a command is built

    In one sentence

    Almost every NetworkPolicy command has the same shape — kubectl, a verb, the networkpolicy type, a name and a namespace — plus a few test commands that run inside pods.

    Template
    kubectl <VERB> networkpolicy <NAME> -n <NAMESPACE> [flags]
    <AMBER> you replace it · [grey] optional · green type exactly

    Every command compared

    CommandReadsWrites files?Talks to cluster?Cluster changes?Card
    explainAPI schemanoyesno5.1
    applyyour filesnoyesyes5.1
    difffiles + live objectstemp filesyesno5.1
    get · describelive objectsnoyesno5.2
    labellive objectsnoyesyes — selection changes5.2
    run · execpodsnoyesprobe pod only5.3
    get policyendpoints · hubbleCNI statenoyesno5.4
    deletelive objectsnoyesyes5.5
