    5.1 · Commands

    Author & apply

    In one sentence

    Write a policy with the schema at hand, preview the change, then apply it.

    kubectl explainread the NetworkPolicy schema from the cluster
    In one sentence

    kubectl explain prints the API documentation for any NetworkPolicy field, straight from the cluster’s schema — the fastest way to check a field name in the exam.

    terminalbash
    kubectl explain networkpolicy.spec.egress.to.ipBlock
    💡 Command hint
    ask the API server / agent→print→nothing sent — cluster unchanged
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • explain print the API schema for a field (works offline from the cluster’s OpenAPI)
    output example outputstdout
    GROUP:      networking.k8s.io
KIND:       NetworkPolicy
VERSION:    v1

FIELD: ipBlock <IPBlock>

DESCRIPTION:
    ipBlock defines policy on a particular IPBlock. If this field is set then
    neither of the other fields can be.

FIELDS:
  cidr	<string> -required-
  except	<[]string>
    ✓ Result
    You know the exact field name, its type and whether it is required.
    ✕ When it fails
    error: field "ipblock" does not exist — field names are case-sensitive (ipBlock).
    Template
    kubectl explain <RESOURCE>[.<FIELD>…]
[--recursive] [--api-version=<GROUP/VERSION>]

    Parameters

    ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
    RESOURCE requiredresource name or short namenetworkpolicy
    netpol    		kubectl explain netpol
    .FIELDdot path into the objectspec.podSelector
    spec.ingress.ports
    spec.egress.to.ipBlock    		kubectl explain netpol.spec.ingress.ports
    --recursiveprint every nested field name at once(flag)kubectl explain netpol.spec --recursive
    --api-versionpick a version when several existnetworking.k8s.io/v1kubectl explain netpol --api-version=networking.k8s.io/v1

    Output

    Group, kind, version, the field description and its child fields with types; -required- marks required fields.

    Watch out

    • Paths use the field names, not list syntax: spec.ingress.from, never spec.ingress[0].from.
    • It reads the schema, not your objects — it never shows live values.

    Examples — by flag, one each

    FlagCommandWhat it shows
    RESOURCEkubectl explain networkpolicytop-level fields of the object
    .FIELDkubectl explain netpol.spec.policyTypesthe docs for one field
    --recursivekubectl explain netpol.spec --recursivethe whole spec tree in one screen
    --api-versionkubectl explain netpol --api-version=networking.k8s.io/v1the v1 schema explicitly

    Examples — by task

    tasks.shbash
    # ── Task: exam — recall the peer fields quickly ──
kubectl explain netpol.spec.ingress.from --recursive

# ── Task: check whether endPort exists on this cluster ──
kubectl explain netpol.spec.egress.ports.endPort
    kubectl applycreate or update policies from files
    In one sentence

    kubectl apply sends your policy files to the API server, which stores them; the CNI enforces them a few seconds later.

    terminalbash
    kubectl apply -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    💡 Command hint
    read the file→API server validates→store in etcd→CNI programs every node
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • apply create the object, or update it if it exists (server keeps a merge record)
    • -f file, folder or URL to read manifests from
    • jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml the manifest file or folder
    output example outputstdout
    networkpolicy.networking.k8s.io/payments-svc-network-policy created
    ✓ Result
    The object is stored and every node is reprogrammed; new connections follow the new rules.
    ✕ When it fails
    The NetworkPolicy "x" is invalid: spec.egress[0].to[0].ipBlock.cidr: Invalid value: "203.0.113.5/24": must be a valid CIDR — the address has host bits; use 203.0.113.0/24.
    Template
    kubectl apply -f <FILE|DIR|URL> [-R]
[-n <NAMESPACE>] [--dry-run=server|client] [--server-side]
[--prune -l <SELECTOR>] [-o name]

    Parameters

    ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
    -f requiredfile, folder or URL with manifestsjahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    jahez-prod/
    https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jahez/…/policy.yaml    		kubectl apply -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    -Ralso read sub-folders of a folder(flag)kubectl apply -f jahez-network-policies/ -R
    -nnamespace for objects that do not set onejahez-prod
    jahez-data    		kubectl apply -f baseline/10-default-deny-all-network-policy.yaml -n jahez-prod
    --dry-runvalidate without saving: server = full API checks, client = local onlyserver
    client    		kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    --server-sidelet the API server merge and track field owners(flag)kubectl apply --server-side -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    --prunedelete live objects no longer in the files (with -l)-l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-network-policieskubectl apply -f jahez-prod/ --prune -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-network-policies
    -ooutput format of the result linesname
    yaml    		kubectl apply -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml -o name

    Output

    One line per object: created, configured (changed) or unchanged.

    Watch out

    • Applying is not enforcing: if the CNI ignores policies, apply still says created.
    • Rules change for new connections; existing long-lived connections may survive until they close.
    • A default-deny applied before the allow policies cuts traffic — apply baseline and service policies in the same sync.

    Examples — by flag, one each

    FlagCommandWhat it shows
    -fkubectl apply -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamlone file
    -Rkubectl apply -f jahez-network-policies/ -Rthe whole repo
    -nkubectl apply -f baseline/10-default-deny-all-network-policy.yaml -n jahez-prodnamespace for objects without one
    --dry-runkubectl apply --dry-run=server -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamlfull validation, nothing stored
    --server-sidekubectl apply --server-side -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamlserver-side merge with field owners
    --prunekubectl apply -f jahez-prod/ --prune -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-network-policiesremoves deleted files’ objects
    -okubectl apply -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml -o nameprints networkpolicy.networking.k8s.io/payments-svc-network-policy

    Examples — by task

    tasks.shbash
    # ── Task: CI — validate every policy in a PR ──
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f jahez-network-policies/ -R

# ── Task: staging — apply then prove it ──
kubectl apply -f jahez-network-policies/ -R
bash jahez-network-policies/tests/verify.sh

# ── Task: emergency — roll back one policy to main ──
git checkout origin/main -- jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
kubectl apply -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    kubectl diffpreview what an apply would change
    In one sentence

    kubectl diff asks the API server what your files would change and prints a unified diff; nothing is saved.

    terminalbash
    kubectl diff -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    💡 Command hint
    read the file→ask the API server→nothing saved — cluster unchanged
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • diff show what apply would change, compared with the live object
    • -f file, folder or URL to read manifests from
    • jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml the manifest file or folder
    output example outputstdout
    diff -u -N /tmp/LIVE-1/networking.k8s.io.v1.NetworkPolicy.jahez-prod.payments-svc-network-policy /tmp/MERGED-1/…
@@ -40,6 +40,9 @@
       ports:
       - port: 5432
         protocol: TCP
+  - to:
+    - ipBlock:
+        cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
    ✓ Result
    You see exactly which rules a PR adds or removes. Exit code 1 means “there are differences”.
    ✕ When it fails
    Exit code >1, e.g. error: unable to recognize — the file is not valid YAML or the kind is unknown.
    Template
    kubectl diff -f <FILE|DIR> [-R]
[--server-side]

    Parameters

    ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
    -f requiredfile or folder to compare with the live objectsjahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    jahez-prod/    		kubectl diff -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml
    -Rinclude sub-folders(flag)kubectl diff -f jahez-network-policies/ -R
    --server-sidecompare using server-side apply(flag)kubectl diff --server-side -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yaml

    Output

    A unified diff per changed object; empty output means no change. Exit code: 0 same, 1 different, >1 error.

    Watch out

    • Generated fields (generation, managedFields) are hidden; only real changes show.
    • Needs the same RBAC as apply, because the server runs a dry-run apply.

    Examples — by flag, one each

    FlagCommandWhat it shows
    -fkubectl diff -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamlthe change for one policy
    -Rkubectl diff -f jahez-network-policies/ -Revery pending change in the repo
    --server-sidekubectl diff --server-side -f jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamldiff as server-side apply would merge

    Examples — by task

    tasks.shbash
    # ── Task: PR review — post the diff as a comment ──
kubectl diff -f jahez-network-policies/ -R > netpol.diff || true

# ── Task: drift check — did someone kubectl-edit prod? ──
kubectl diff -f jahez-network-policies/ -R && echo "no drift"

    Inspect

    In one sentence

    Read what is live and check that every selector really matches the pods you expect.

    kubectl get networkpolicylist policies and their selectors
    In one sentence

    kubectl get networkpolicy lists the policies in a namespace with the pods they select — the first command when a connection times out.

    terminalbash
    kubectl get networkpolicy -n jahez-prod
    💡 Command hint
    ask the API server / agent→print→nothing sent — cluster unchanged
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • get list objects from the API server
    • networkpolicy the resource type (short names: netpol, networkpolicies)
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • jahez-prod namespace value
    output example outputstdout
    NAME                              POD-SELECTOR                              AGE
allow-dns-network-policy          <none>                                    41d
api-gateway-network-policy        app.kubernetes.io/name=api-gateway        41d
default-deny-all-network-policy   <none>                                    41d
orders-svc-network-policy         app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-svc         41d
payments-svc-network-policy       app.kubernetes.io/name=payments-svc       3m
    ✓ Result
    You see every policy and which pods it protects. <none> means podSelector: {} — all pods.
    ✕ When it fails
    No resources found in jahez-prod namespace. — no policy exists, so every pod is open.
    Template
    kubectl get networkpolicy [<NAME>]
[-n <NAMESPACE> | -A] [-l <SELECTOR>]
[-o wide|yaml|json|name|jsonpath=<EXPR>] [--sort-by=<EXPR>] [--watch]

    Parameters

    ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
    NAMEone policy; omit for allpayments-svc-network-policykubectl get netpol payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod
    -nnamespacejahez-prod
    jahez-data
    monitoring    		kubectl get netpol -n jahez-data
    -Aevery namespace(flag)kubectl get netpol -A
    -lfilter policies by their own labelsapp.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-checkoutkubectl get netpol -n jahez-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-checkout
    -ooutput formatwide
    yaml
    json
    name
    jsonpath={.items[*].metadata.name}    		kubectl get netpol payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod -o yaml
    --sort-bysort by a field.metadata.creationTimestampkubectl get netpol -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
    --watchstream changes(flag)kubectl get netpol -n jahez-prod --watch

    Output

    NAME, POD-SELECTOR and AGE. There is no READY or STATUS column — NetworkPolicy has no status.

    Watch out

    • -l filters the policies’ labels, not the pods they select.
    • A listed policy can still select zero pods (typo in a label) — check with kubectl get pods -l.

    Examples — by flag, one each

    FlagCommandWhat it shows

    -okubectl get netpol payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod -o yamlthe full live object
    --sort-bykubectl get netpol -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestampnewest last — what changed recently

  [ "$(kubectl get netpol -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)" = 0 ] && echo "OPEN: $ns"
done

# ── Task: script — names only, as JSON ──

    kubectl describe networkpolicyread a policy in plain words
    In one sentence

    kubectl describe rewrites a policy as sentences — which pods, which sources and destinations, which ports — making AND/OR mistakes easy to spot.

    terminalbash
    kubectl describe networkpolicy payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod
    💡 Command hint
    ask the API server / agent→print→nothing sent — cluster unchanged
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • describe print a human summary of the object, including selectors and rules
    • networkpolicy the resource type (short names: netpol, networkpolicies)
    • payments-svc-network-policy the NetworkPolicy name (ends with its kind)
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • jahez-prod namespace value
    output example outputstdout
    Name:         payments-svc-network-policy
Namespace:    jahez-prod
Spec:
  PodSelector:     app.kubernetes.io/name=payments-svc
  Allowing ingress traffic:
    To Port: 8080/TCP
    From:
      PodSelector: app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-svc
    ----------
    To Port: 9090/TCP
    From:
      NamespaceSelector: kubernetes.io/metadata.name=monitoring
      PodSelector: app.kubernetes.io/name=prometheus
  Allowing egress traffic:
    To Port: 5432/TCP
    To:
      NamespaceSelector: kubernetes.io/metadata.name=jahez-data
      PodSelector: app.kubernetes.io/name=payments-db
  Policy Types: Ingress, Egress
    ✓ Result
    Selectors that appear under the same From: are ANDed; separate From: entries are ORed.
    ✕ When it fails
    Error from server (NotFound): networkpolicies.networking.k8s.io "payments-svc" not found — use the full name ending in -network-policy.
    Template
    kubectl describe networkpolicy [<NAME>]
[-n <NAMESPACE> | -A] [-l <SELECTOR>]

    Parameters

    ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
    NAMEone policy; omit to describe all in the namespacepayments-svc-network-policykubectl describe netpol payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod
    -nnamespacejahez-prod
    monitoring    		kubectl describe netpol -n monitoring
    -Aevery namespace(flag)kubectl describe netpol -A
    -lonly policies with these labelsapp.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-checkoutkubectl describe netpol -n jahez-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-checkout

    Output

    Name, namespace, the pod selector, each ingress and egress rule (ports, then peers), and the policy types. Events are always empty.

    Watch out

    • “Allowing ingress traffic: <none> (Selected pods are isolated for ingress connectivity)” means deny-all in that direction.
    • describe does not tell you whether any pod matches the selector.

    Examples — by flag, one each

    FlagCommandWhat it shows
    NAMEkubectl describe netpol payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prodone policy in sentences
    -nkubectl describe netpol -n monitoringall monitoring policies
    -Akubectl describe netpol -Aeverything — for a full review
    -lkubectl describe netpol -n jahez-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=jahez-checkoutonly checkout policies

    Examples — by task

    tasks.shbash
    # ── Task: incident — why can't the gateway reach payments? ──
kubectl describe netpol payments-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod | sed -n '/ingress/,/egress/p'
kubectl describe netpol api-gateway-network-policy -n jahez-prod | sed -n '/egress/,$p'
    kubectl get pods -l / kubectl labelcheck and change the labels policies select
    In one sentence

    Policies select labels, so kubectl get pods -l proves who a selector matches, and kubectl label changes who it matches — instantly.

    terminalbash
    kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=payments-svc --show-labels
    💡 Command hint
    ask the API server / agent→print→nothing sent — cluster unchanged
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • get list objects from the API server
    • pods the resource type pod
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • jahez-prod namespace value
    • -l label selector — only objects whose labels match
    • --show-labels add a LABELS column
    output example outputstdout
    NAME                                     READY   STATUS    LABELS
payments-svc-deployment-84f6d7c5b-t3v6x   1/1     Running   app.kubernetes.io/name=payments-svc,pod-template-hash=84f6d7c5b,tier=backend
payments-svc-deployment-84f6d7c5b-w8p1c   1/1     Running   app.kubernetes.io/name=payments-svc,pod-template-hash=84f6d7c5b,tier=backend
    ✓ Result
    Two pods match — the payments policy protects exactly these two.
    ✕ When it fails
    No resources found — the selector matches nothing; the policy protects no pod (typo or wrong label key).
    Template
    kubectl get pods -n <NAMESPACE> -l <SELECTOR> [--show-labels]
kubectl get ns --show-labels
kubectl label <TYPE> <NAME> <KEY>=<VALUE> [--overwrite] [-n <NAMESPACE>]

    Test connectivity

    In one sentence

    A policy is only proven by a real connection: test allowed flows (open) and denied flows (timed out) from the right identity.

    kubectl run (probe pod)start a throw-away pod to test a flow
    In one sentence

    kubectl run starts a probe pod with the labels you choose, so you can test exactly what a policy allows for a given identity.

    terminalbash
    kubectl run netshoot-probe-pod -n jahez-prod --rm -it --restart=Never --image=nicolaka/netshoot --labels=app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-svc -- nc -zv -w 3 payments-svc 8080
    💡 Command hint
    start a shell in a pod→send a real packet→policy decides: allowed or dropped
    • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
    • run start a one-off pod (here: a probe pod for testing)
    • -n the namespace to work in
    • jahez-prod namespace value
    • --rm delete the pod when the command exits
    • -it interactive terminal
    • --restart=Never create a bare Pod, not a Deployment
    • --image=nicolaka/netshoot container image for the probe pod
    • --labels=app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-svc labels for the probe pod — they decide which policies apply to it
    • -- everything after this goes to the command inside the container
    • nc network tool run inside the pod
    • -zv scan + verbose: report whether the TCP port opened (nc)
    • -w wait timeout in seconds (nc)
    • 3 port / number
    • 8080 port / number
    output example outputstdout
    payments-svc (172.20.91.3:8080) open
pod "netshoot-probe-pod" deleted

    A pod wearing the orders label may reach payments — the policy works for that identity.
    ✕ When it fails
    Operation timed out — some egress or ingress rule is missing; go to 5.6.

    Four ways to test

    1️⃣ Manual probe with netshoot

    Spin a debug pod with the labels of the source you want to simulate, then curl -m 3 the target. Failure = drop.

    2️⃣ cyclonus & kubectl-np-viewer

    Open-source tools that enumerate your policies and tell you the effective allow-matrix.

    3️⃣ CNI-native flow logs

    Cilium's hubble observe, Calico's calicoctl flow logs — show every accepted/denied flow in real time.

    4️⃣ Synthetic test pods

    Permanent canary pods with known labels in CI that probe their expected paths every minute. Alert when expected flows fail or unexpected ones succeed.

    The probe pattern

    probe.sh — the bash idiom you'll use weeklybash
    # Should succeed: gateway → orders
kubectl run probe-from-gateway -n jahez-prod \
  --labels=app.kubernetes.io/name=api-gateway \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
  curl -m 3 -sf http://orders-svc:8080/health

# Should fail: cart → payments (not in matrix)
kubectl run probe-from-cart -n jahez-prod \
  --labels=app.kubernetes.io/name=cart-svc \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
  curl -m 3 -sf http://payments-svc:8080/health
# expected: timeout / connection refused

# Should fail: any pod → cloud metadata
kubectl run probe-imds -n jahez-prod \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
  curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
# expected: timeout

    Troubleshooting

    In one sentence

    Read the error first — bad address, timed out or refused each point to a different stage — then check that stage’s policy.

    Where each error is raised
    #What you seeStageCauseFix
    1nc: bad address 'payments-svc'DNSegress isolated, kube-dns not allowed (or only UDP)allow kube-dns on UDP and TCP 53 (4.4)
    2Operation timed out from the sendersrc egressno egress rule on the sender matches destination + portadd the destination to the sender’s egress
    3timeout only across nodes / to RDSwire / SGAWS security group or NACL blocks it, not the policycheck the node / pod security groups
    4Operation timed out, sender’s egress is finedst ingressno ingress rule on the receiver lists this sourceadd the source to the receiver’s ingress
    5Connection refusedapp portpacket arrived; nothing listens on that portnot a policy problem — check the containerPort / Service targetPort

    The "where did the packet die?" flowchart

    Debugging a "connection refused" mystery
    1 / 5

    Step 1 — Reproduce in a probe pod

    Forget the application. Spin a netshoot pod with the same labels as the failing source pod, then curl -v the target. If this works but your app fails, it's an app bug; if this fails, it's a policy issue.

    Step 2 — List policies that select source & target

    kubectl get netpol -n jahez-prod -o json | \
  jq '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector.matchLabels."app.kubernetes.io/name" == "orders-svc")'

    Both source's egress policies AND target's ingress policies must permit the flow.

    Step 3 — Check policyTypes & rules carefully

    Common bugs: policyTypes: [Ingress] when you meant both. A peer that's a namespaceSelector alone (matches all pods in matching NS — usually fine) versus combined with podSelector (AND, much narrower).

    Step 4 — Verify the labels

    kubectl get pod -n jahez-prod orders-svc-xxxx --show-labels

    If the pod is missing app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-svc, the policy doesn't match it — which means default-allow if no other policy selects it, or default-deny if some other catch-all selects it.

    Step 5 — Tap the CNI

    Cilium: hubble observe --from-pod jahez-prod/orders-svc-xxxx --verdict DROPPED.

    Calico: calicoctl get globalnetworkset + flow logs.

    If the CNI says "no policy match — implicit deny", the source/target labels don't match what your policy expects. If it says "denied by policy X", you know which manifest to fix.

    The ten common pitfalls

    Every team that has rolled out NetworkPolicies in production has hit at least five of these. Here they are, ranked roughly by how often they bite.

    ① Forgetting to allow DNS

    You apply default-deny-egress, the app starts timing out on every named lookup. The single most common break. Always pair default-deny with allow-DNS to kube-system/k8s-app=kube-dns.

    ② Your CNI doesn't enforce policies

    Flannel-only clusters, AKS without --network-policy, EKS without VPC CNI policy support — the YAMLs apply cleanly but nothing happens. Test with a known-deny rule and verify it actually blocks.

    ③ AND vs OR confusion in peers

    Putting podSelector and namespaceSelector as keys of the same dashed entry = AND (specific pods in specific NS). As separate dashed entries = OR. People write OR when they mean AND, accidentally allowing all pods in the source NS.

    ④ Inferred policyTypes surprises

    If you only set spec.egress, Kubernetes infers policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] — which means ingress also gets locked down to nothing. Always set policyTypes explicitly.

    ⑤ policyTypes: [Ingress] + leaving egress wide open

    You secure ingress meticulously, then forget that egress is still default-allow. A compromised pod still has full egress to the internet, the metadata service, and every other pod's metrics port.

    ⑥ Missing 169.254.169.254 carve-out

    Open-internet egress policies that don't except: 169.254.169.254/32 let SSRF in any pod steal IAM credentials from IMDS. Always except the metadata service.

    ⑦ Cluster mesh / multi-cluster blind spots

    If you use Cilium ClusterMesh / Submariner / Istio multi-cluster, traffic from another cluster appears with foreign IPs that no podSelector can match. Use cluster-aware peers (Cilium fromGroups) or ipBlock by remote pod CIDR.

    ⑧ Hostnetwork pods bypass policies

    Pods with spec.hostNetwork: true use the node's network namespace and are not subject to NetworkPolicy on most CNIs. Audit for this — it's how some agents (node-exporter) and some sneaky workloads escape.

    ⑨ Service IPs vs Pod IPs in ipBlock

    NetworkPolicy ipBlock filters pod IPs, not Service ClusterIPs. After kube-proxy rewrites destination, the policy sees the pod IP. Don't try to ipBlock the Service VIP — it won't match.

    ⑩ "Just for now" wide-open rules that never get tightened

    Someone debugs an issue by adding {} # allow all as a temporary measure. The TODO never gets done. Audit policies in CI for empty selectors and `0.0.0.0/0` without exceptions; fail builds.

    Practices & labs

    The full Jahez project, exam-style labs and the cheat sheet.

    6Jahez project
    6.1 · Jahez project

    Architecture & traffic matrix

    In one sentence

    Ten services, four data stores and four namespaces — every allowed flow drawn, numbered and listed before a single policy is written.

    A complete, deployable example. We will build NetworkPolicies for a realistic e-commerce platform with an API gateway, six microservices, three databases, a cache, a message broker, and observability — then progressively lock it down to zero-trust.

    The system at a glance

    The fictional Jahez e-commerce stack consists of public web traffic entering through an Ingress controller, hitting an API gateway, which fans out to six business services. Each service owns its own data store. A central observability namespace scrapes everything; an internal admin tool sits in its own namespace. Three external endpoints are reachable: the payment provider, an SMS gateway, and an object storage bucket.

    Fig P1.1 — Full Jahez e-commerce architecture: 4 namespaces, 6 services, 4 databases, external dependencies

    The request flow — every pod, every namespace, every wire

    This is the complete L3/L4 traffic graph for the Jahez stack. Every box is a real pod; every line is a real allowed connection. Arrows use a fixed two-color convention so you can trace ingress and egress at a glance:

    🟢 Green arrows = INGRESS direction

    The arrow lands on a pod's ingress side — answers "who is allowed to arrive at this pod?". Every green arrowhead is a permission listed in the destination pod's spec.ingress rules.

    🔵 Blue arrows = EGRESS direction

    The arrow leaves a pod's egress side — answers "where is this pod allowed to reach?". Every blue arrow tail is a permission listed in the source pod's spec.egress rules.

    Because every wire is both — egress from the sender, ingress to the receiver — each line in the diagram below is drawn with a blue tail and a green head: blue where it leaves the source, transitioning to green where it arrives at the destination. If you follow any line backward (green → blue) you see the policy pair that allows it: the destination's ingress rule (green end) plus the source's egress rule (blue end). Both must exist for the packet to flow.

    Fig P1.2 — Complete request flow. Every line is one allowed wire: blue dot at the source (egress) → fading into green arrow at the destination (ingress). 24 numbered flows · 4 namespaces · 13 pods · 3 external endpoints.

    Reading the flow — one customer order, end to end

    Trace what happens when a single customer places an order, in the order the packets fire. Each step crosses one or two policies:

    #StepWireEgress sideIngress side
    ①Customer hits Jahez.sainternet → ingress-nginx :443(no source policy)ingress-nginx LB
    ②L7 routingingress-nginx → api-gateway :8080ingress-nginx-egressapi-gateway-network-policy · ingress
    ③Build the pageapi-gateway → catalog-svc :8080api-gateway-network-policy · egresscatalog-svc-network-policy · ingress
    ④Read user profileapi-gateway → users-svc :8080api-gateway-network-policy · egressusers-svc-network-policy · ingress
    ⑤Fetch cartapi-gateway → cart-svc :8080api-gateway-network-policy · egresscart-svc-network-policy · ingress
    ⑥Cart hits Rediscart-svc → redis :6379cart-svc-network-policy · egressredis-network-policy · ingress
    ⑦Place the orderapi-gateway → orders-svc :8080api-gateway-network-policy · egressorders-svc-network-policy · ingress
    ⑧Validate line itemsorders-svc → catalog-svc :8080orders-svc-network-policy · egresscatalog-svc-network-policy · ingress
    ⑨Charge the customerorders-svc → payments-svc :8080orders-svc-network-policy · egresspayments-svc-network-policy · ingress
    ⑩Call Madapayments-svc → 203.0.113.0/24 :443payments-svc-network-policy · egress (ipBlock)(external)
    ⑪Persist paymentpayments-svc → payments-db :5432payments-svc-network-policy · egresspayments-db-network-policy · ingress
    ⑫Persist orderorders-svc → orders-db :5432orders-svc-network-policy · egressorders-db-network-policy · ingress
    ⑬Publish eventorders-svc → rabbitmq :5672orders-svc-network-policy · egressrabbitmq-network-policy · ingress
    ⑭Notify worker consumesnotify-svc → rabbitmq :5672notify-svc-network-policy · egressrabbitmq-network-policy · ingress
    ⑮Send SMSnotify-svc → 192.0.2.0/24 :443notify-svc-network-policy · egress (ipBlock)(external)
    ⑯Upload invoicenotify-svc → S3 :443notify-svc-network-policy · egress (ipBlock)(external)

    Sixteen packets, sixteen policy pairs, zero gaps. If any single one of those policies is missing or misconfigured, the order fails — and that's exactly what you want from a security control: noisy failures in your testing, not silent leaks in production.

    How to read any line in the diagram. Find the line. Look at where the blue dot is — that pod's NetworkPolicy must list this destination in its spec.egress. Follow to where the green arrowhead lands — that pod's NetworkPolicy must list the source in its spec.ingress. Both must exist or the kernel drops the SYN.

    The traffic matrix — who talks to whom

    This matrix is the source of truth for every NetworkPolicy that follows. If a flow isn't here, it doesn't exist. If you spot one missing, that's a security review finding.

    From ↓ / To →gatewaycatalogorderspaymentsuserscartnotifyredisrabbitDBsexternal
    ingress-nginx:8080——————————
    api-gateway—:8080:8080—:8080:8080—————
    catalog-svc—————————catalog-db:27017—
    orders-svc—:8080—:8080————:5672orders-db:5432—
    payments-svc————————:5672payments-db:5432Mada :443
    users-svc—————————users-db:5432—
    cart-svc—:8080—————:6379———
    notify-svc————————:5672 (consume)—Unifonic :443, S3 :443
    prometheus:9090:9090:9090:9090:9090:9090:9090:9121:15692:9187 (PG exp)—

    Every cell that says "—" is a flow we will actively deny. Every cell that has a port is a flow we will explicitly allow. The job of NetworkPolicies in this project is to mechanically translate this matrix into manifests.

    6.2 · Jahez project

    Namespaces & labels

    In one sentence

    Namespaces and pod labels come first, because every selector in every policy depends on them.

    Before any policy, the namespaces and their labels. Get this right and every policy below "just works"; get it wrong and you'll spend hours debugging selectors that match nothing.

    Four namespaces

    00-namespaces.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: jahez-prod
  labels:
    name: jahez-prod           # custom label
    env: prod
    tier: application
    # kubernetes.io/metadata.name=jahez-prod is auto-set since 1.22
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: jahez-data
  labels:
    name: jahez-data
    env: prod
    tier: data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: monitoring
  labels:
    name: monitoring
    tier: platform
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: ingress-nginx          # where the L7 ingress runs
  labels:
    name: ingress-nginx
    tier: platform

    Pod label conventions

    Every workload Deployment in this project sets at minimum these labels:

    label-convention.yaml — used by every DeploymentYAML
    labels:
  app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc          # unique service identifier
  app.kubernetes.io/component: api             # api | worker | db | cache | broker
  app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jahez-checkout     # bounded context grouping
  tier: backend                                # frontend | backend | data
  env: prod
    Why this matters. Throughout the policies below we use app.kubernetes.io/name as the primary selector key. If you forget to set it on a pod, the policy targeting that pod will simply not match — and the pod will be silently broken (allowed everywhere, since no policy selects it). Make label discipline a deploy-time admission constraint (Kyverno / Gatekeeper).
    6.3 · Jahez project

    Default-deny baseline

    In one sentence

    Lay the floor before anything else: deny all in every namespace, then give DNS back.

    Before any business logic, lay down the default-deny floor. Three policies, one per workload-bearing namespace. After this is applied, your cluster is broken — every pod loses connectivity. We rebuild it back deliberately, flow by flow.

    baseline/10-default-deny-all-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all-network-policy
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]

    Cluster-wide allow-DNS (apply per namespace)

    baseline/11-allow-dns-network-policy.yamlYAML
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---
# Repeat the same NetworkPolicy in jahez-data and monitoring,
# changing only `metadata.namespace`. Every workload-bearing NS
# needs DNS allowed once the default-deny is in place.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
spec:

        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---

    State after P3. Every pod in jahez-prod, jahez-data, monitoring is fully isolated except they can do DNS lookups. They can't talk to each other. They can't talk to the internet. They can't even talk to themselves cross-pod. This is the secure floor we now build allow-rules on top of.

    Verifying the floor

    tests/verify.shbash
    # Spin a debug pod inside jahez-prod
kubectl run debug -n jahez-prod --rm -it \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- bash

# Inside the pod — every check should fail (timeout) except DNS
nslookup kubernetes.default                 # ✓ works (DNS allowed)
curl -m 3 https://www.google.com            # ✗ timeout (no internet egress)
curl -m 3 http://orders-svc.jahez-prod      # ✗ timeout (no pod-to-pod yet)
curl -m 3 http://prometheus.monitoring:9090 # ✗ timeout (cross-NS denied)
    ⌘ Commands for this file
    bash tests/verify.sh
    run the checks
    💡 Command hint
    run on your machine→print
      6.4 · Jahez project

      API gateway

      In one sentence

      The gateway is the only pod ingress-nginx may reach, and it may call only the four front services.

      The api-gateway is the only pod that the ingress-nginx controller is allowed to reach. Its policy declares: ingress from ingress-nginx namespace only, egress to the four backend services it routes to.

      Gateway Deployment (for completeness)

      api-gateway-deployment.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-gateway-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway
    app.kubernetes.io/component: gateway
    tier: frontend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway
        app.kubernetes.io/component: gateway
        tier: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/api-gateway:1.4.2
          ports:
            - { name: http, containerPort: 8080 }
            - { name: metrics, containerPort: 9090 }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }

      Gateway NetworkPolicy

      Fig P4.1 — api-gateway policy: 2 ingress sources, 4 service egress destinations + DNS. Payments and databases deliberately omitted.
      jahez-prod/20-api-gateway-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-gateway-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # [1] Public traffic enters via ingress-nginx
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
    # [2] Prometheus scrapes /metrics
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }
  egress:
    # [3] Routes to catalog-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [4] Routes to orders-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [5] Routes to users-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: users-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [6] Routes to cart-svc
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: cart-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # Note: gateway does NOT call payments-svc directly — that's orders' job
    # Note: gateway does NOT call notify-svc — that's async via rabbitmq

      Ingress controller policy (in ingress-nginx namespace)

      The ingress-nginx pods themselves need to be reachable from the internet (LoadBalancer service) and need egress to the gateway. We add a focused egress policy in the controller's namespace.

      ingress-nginx/21-ingress-nginx-egress-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: ingress-nginx-egress-network-policy
  namespace: ingress-nginx
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # DNS — even ingress-nginx needs it for upstream resolution
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

      6.5 · Jahez project

      Catalog

      In one sentence

      Catalog accepts three callers through one In expression and talks only to its MongoDB.

      Catalog is the simplest backend in the system. It serves product reads to the gateway, the orders service (for line-item validation), and the cart service (for price + stock checks). It only talks to its MongoDB database. No external egress.

      Fig P5.1 — catalog-svc policy: 3 service callers (OR via matchExpressions) + Prometheus; egress to Mongo only.
      jahez-prod/30-catalog-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: catalog-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # Three internal callers — using matchExpressions for OR
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: app.kubernetes.io/name, operator: In,
                  values: [api-gateway, orders-svc, cart-svc] }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # Prometheus scrape
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # Only to the catalog MongoDB in jahez-data
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-db }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 27017 }]
    # DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

      matchExpressions for OR. The ingress block uses matchExpressions with operator: In to match any of three different upstream callers in a single rule — equivalent to three separate dashed entries but more compact.
      6.6 · Jahez project

      Orders

      In one sentence

      Orders has one caller and five dependencies — each one an egress rule.

      Orders takes the gateway request, validates the cart against catalog, calls payments to charge, persists the order in PostgreSQL, and publishes an event to RabbitMQ for notify-svc to pick up. Five distinct egress flows; one ingress source.

      Fig P6.1 — orders-svc connection map: 1 ingress (gateway) + 5 egress (catalog, payments, db, rabbit, dns)
      jahez-prod/40-orders-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: api-gateway }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # [1] catalog-svc — line-item validation
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: catalog-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [2] payments-svc — charge the customer
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    # [3] orders-db (Postgres in jahez-data)
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    # [4] rabbitmq — publish OrderCreated event
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # [5] DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

      6.7 · Jahez project

      Payments (PCI)

      In one sentence

      Payments accepts only orders and is the only service allowed to reach the payment provider.

      Payments is the most security-sensitive pod in the cluster. It is the only pod permitted egress to an external payment provider (Mada / HyperPay CIDR). It writes to its own Postgres. It accepts traffic only from orders-svc and prometheus.

      🔒 PCI-DSS scope reduction

      By placing payments in its own labelled set with a tight policy that only allows traffic from orders-svc and only allows egress to one Mada CIDR + one DB, you can argue to auditors that the PCI scope is well-defined.

      Fig P7.1 — payments-svc: orders-only ingress, 4 egress destinations including external ipBlock for the payment provider.
      jahez-prod/50-payments-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-svc-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    jahez.sa/pci-scope: "true"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # Only orders-svc can call payments — gateway cannot
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # [1] payments-db (Postgres in jahez-data)
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-data }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-db }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    # [2] rabbitmq — publish PaymentSucceeded / PaymentFailed
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # [3] External payment provider — Mada / HyperPay
    # Get the actual CIDRs from your provider; these are illustrative
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 198.51.100.0/24
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]
    # [4] DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

      6.8 · Jahez project

      Data tier

      In one sentence

      Each data store accepts only its own service from jahez-prod, plus its replicas and the metrics exporter.

      The data tier is the easiest to write because the rules are short — but the highest-leverage to get right. A leaky database policy is how a compromised pod ends up reading every customer's payment history.

      The four databases (in jahez-data)

      Fig P8.1 — orders-db: 1 service caller (cross-NS), Prometheus exporter, self-peer for replication. No external egress.
      Fig P8.2 — catalog-db: identical pattern to Postgres but with port 27017 and full read/write traffic from catalog-svc.
      jahez-data/60-databases-network-policy.yamlYAML
      ################################################################
# orders-db (Postgres) — only orders-svc can connect
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-db-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-data
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: jahez-prod }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    # Postgres exporter scraped by Prometheus
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9187 }]
    # Replica → primary streaming replication
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
  egress:
    # DNS only — Postgres needs no other egress
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    # Replica peer egress
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-db
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
---

      Redis cache (cart) and RabbitMQ broker

      Both live in jahez-prod alongside the apps. Redis serves cart-svc; RabbitMQ has multiple producers (orders, payments) and one consumer (notify).

      Fig P8.3 — redis (single producer/consumer) vs rabbitmq (multi-producer + cluster peering). Note rabbit's matchExpressions In ingress + same-label peer egress for Erlang dist.
      jahez-prod/61-redis-rabbitmq-network-policy.yamlYAML
      ################################################################
# Redis — only cart-svc on 6379
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: redis-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: redis }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: cart-svc }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 6379 }]
    # redis_exporter sidecar metrics, scraped by Prom
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9121 }]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---
################################################################
# RabbitMQ — accepts from orders, payments, notify; clusters on 25672
################################################################
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: rabbitmq-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # AMQP producers/consumers
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: app.kubernetes.io/name, operator: In,
                  values: [orders-svc, payments-svc, notify-svc] }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # Cluster peering between rabbit pods (Erlang dist + epmd)
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 25672 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 4369 }
    # Prometheus scrape
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 15692 }]
  egress:
    # Cluster peer egress + DNS
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 25672 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 4369 }
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

      Stateful clustering pattern. Notice both Postgres replication, Mongo replica set, and RabbitMQ clustering use the same trick: an ingress rule that selects pods with the same label as the pod itself. This is how StatefulSet pods talk to each other — they all share the label and allow each other.
      6.9 · Jahez project

      Users · cart · notify

      In one sentence

      notify-svc — the only service with broad external egress

      notify-svc consumes from RabbitMQ, sends SMS via Unifonic, and uploads invoices to S3. Two external CIDR allows + carve-outs.

      Fig P9.3 — notify-svc: zero application ingress, broad egress (rabbitmq pull, SMS gateway, S3 invoices).
      jahez-prod/72-notify-svc-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: notify-svc-network-policy, namespace: jahez-prod }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: notify-svc }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # notify-svc is async — only Prom scrapes it
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # RabbitMQ — consume events
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rabbitmq }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5672 }]
    # Unifonic SMS gateway
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 192.0.2.0/24
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]
    # S3 — invoices & receipts (broad egress with carve-outs)
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 198.18.0.0/24      # S3 me-central-1 — placeholder; use the com.amazonaws.me-central-1.s3 prefix list
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 198.18.1.0/24
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]
    # DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

      6.10 · Jahez project

      Observability

      In one sentence

      Prometheus needs the widest reach and the API server by its real endpoint IPs; Grafana accepts only the VPN.

      Prometheus is the chattiest pod in the cluster — by design. It must be allowed to egress to every workload's metrics port. Grafana queries Prometheus and receives ingress from the company VPN CIDR. Loki tails logs.

      Prometheus — wide egress to all scrape targets

      Fig P10.1 — prometheus: one ingress (grafana), seven egress destinations (cross-NS scrapes + control plane).
      monitoring/80-prometheus-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: prometheus-network-policy, namespace: monitoring }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    # Grafana queries Prometheus
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: grafana }
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }]
  egress:
    # [1] scrape any workload pod in jahez-prod or jahez-data
    # — note: cross-NS, broad. Restrict ports to known scrape ports
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - { key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name, operator: In,
                  values: [jahez-prod, jahez-data, ingress-nginx] }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9090 }   # app metrics
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9187 }   # postgres_exporter
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9121 }   # redis_exporter
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 15692 }  # rabbit prom plugin
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 10254 }  # nginx-ingress metrics
    # [2] DNS
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
    # [3] kube-apiserver — for service discovery
    # ipBlock sees the address AFTER kube-proxy DNAT, so list the real endpoints,
    # not the 10.96.0.1 Service VIP:  kubectl get endpoints kubernetes -n default
    - to:
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.12.34/32 }    # EKS control-plane ENI · me-central-1a
        - ipBlock: { cidr: 10.50.140.21/32 }   # EKS control-plane ENI · me-central-1b
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]

      Project complete. With these 10 parts applied, every flow in the matrix from §P1 is explicitly allowed; every flow not in the matrix is implicitly denied by the default-deny baseline. Compromise of any single pod cannot reach databases or peers it doesn't already need.
      Fixed in v5. The API-server rule now lists the control-plane endpoint IPs. The old ipBlock: 10.96.0.1/32 never matched, because policies see addresses after Service DNAT (4.6).
      7CKAD labs
      7.1 · CKAD labs

      Six labs with solutions

      In one sentence

      Six exam-style tasks on a jahez-lab namespace; try each one first, then open the solution.

      Lab 1 · Default-deny a namespace, keep DNS

      In namespace jahez-lab, block all ingress and egress for every pod, but keep DNS lookups working. Name the policies default-deny-all-network-policy and allow-dns-network-policy.

      Show solution

      What you will build

      Setup

      setup.shbash
      kubectl create namespace jahez-lab
kubectl create deployment menu-api-deployment -n jahez-lab --image=nginx:1.27 --port=80
kubectl label deployment menu-api-deployment -n jahez-lab app=menu-api --overwrite
kubectl expose deployment menu-api-deployment -n jahez-lab --name=menu-api-service --port=80

      Full YAML

      lab1-network-policies.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-lab
spec:
  # ① Who is protected?  every pod
  podSelector: {}
  # ② Which directions?  both — no rules means nothing allowed
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-lab
spec:
  # ① Who is protected?  every pod
  podSelector: {}
  # ② Which directions?
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  # ④ Where may it go?  kube-dns only
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }

      Lab 5 · Internet egress with carve-outs

      Pods app=notify-worker may reach any internet address on TCP 443, but never the node metadata service (169.254.169.254) or private ranges.

kubectl exec -n jahez-lab deploy/notify-worker-deployment -- curl -sS -m 3 -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://example.com
kubectl exec -n jahez-lab deploy/notify-worker-deployment -- curl -sS -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
      output example outputstdout
      200
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3001 milliseconds

      Exam traps

      • Every except range must sit inside cidr.
      • On EKS the VPC (10.50.0.0/16) is inside 10.0.0.0/8 — this also blocks other pods by IP, which is intended here.
      Lab 6 · Fix the broken policy

      This policy should let only Prometheus (in monitoring) scrape menu-api, and keep menu-api’s egress isolated. It does neither. Find both bugs and fix them.

      Show solution

      What you will build

      Setup

      setup.shbash
      cat > lab6-broken.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: menu-api-scrape-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-lab
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: menu-api }
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9113 }
EOF

      Full YAML

      lab6-fixed-network-policy.yamlYAML
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: menu-api-scrape-network-policy
  namespace: jahez-lab
spec:
  # ① Who is protected?
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: menu-api }
  # ② Which directions?  bug 2: without this only Ingress is isolated
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  # ③ Who may come in?  bug 1: one peer (no second dash) = AND
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9113 }
  # ④ Where may it go?  nothing listed here; lab 4's policy adds menu-db + DNS
  egress: []
      ⌘ Commands for this file
      kubectl apply -f lab6-fixed-network-policy.yaml
      create the policies
      💡 Command hint
      read the file→API server validates→store in etcd→CNI programs every node
      • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
      • apply create the object, or update it if it exists (server keeps a merge record)
      • -f file, folder or URL to read manifests from
      • lab6-fixed-network-policy.yaml the manifest file or folder
      kubectl get netpol -n jahez-lab
      list them
      💡 Command hint
      ask the API server / agent→print→nothing sent — cluster unchanged
      • kubectl the Kubernetes CLI — talks to the API server using your kubeconfig
      • get list objects from the API server
      • netpol short name for networkpolicy
      • -n the namespace to work in

      Verify

      verify.shbash
      kubectl apply -f lab6-fixed-network-policy.yaml
kubectl describe netpol menu-api-scrape-network-policy -n jahez-lab | grep -A6 "Allowing ingress"
kubectl get netpol menu-api-scrape-network-policy -n jahez-lab -o jsonpath="{.spec.policyTypes}"
      output example outputstdout
        Allowing ingress traffic:
    To Port: 9113/TCP
    From:
      NamespaceSelector: kubernetes.io/metadata.name=monitoring
      PodSelector: app.kubernetes.io/name=prometheus
["Ingress","Egress"]

      Exam traps

      • In the broken file, any pod in monitoring and any prometheus-labelled pod in jahez-lab could connect.
      • egress: [] adds nothing; the union with lab 4 still allows menu-db and DNS.
      8Cheat sheet
      8.1 · Cheat sheet

      Snippets · one-liners · rollout

      In one sentence

      The snippets and one-liners you will copy most, plus the order to roll policies out safely.

      The single page you'll reference forever. Copy/paste-ready snippets and the kubectl one-liners that matter.

      Snippet library

      GoalSnippet
      Default-deny-all in NSpodSelector: {} · policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
      Allow DNS to kube-dnsegress to ns kube-system, k8s-app=kube-dns, UDP/53 + TCP/53
      Allow ingress from same NSfrom: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: foo}}}]
      Allow ingress cross-NS (specific pods)from: [{namespaceSelector: ..., podSelector: ...}] (AND)
      Allow ingress from any pod in another NSfrom: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring}}}]
      Allow egress to internet (with carveouts)ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0, except: [10.0.0.0/8, 169.254.169.254/32]}
      Allow Prometheus to scrapeingress from monitoring/prometheus on metrics port

      kubectl one-liners

      kubectl-cheatsheet.shbash
      # List all NetworkPolicies in a namespace
kubectl get netpol -n jahez-prod

# Describe a policy in human-readable form
kubectl describe netpol orders-svc-network-policy -n jahez-prod

# See exactly which pods a policy selects
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-svc

# Apply all manifests in a directory
kubectl apply -f ./netpol/ --recursive

# Dry-run validate before apply
kubectl apply -f orders-svc-netpol.yaml --dry-run=server

# Quick ephemeral debug pod
kubectl run debug -n jahez-prod \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it --restart=Never -- bash

# Check Cilium dropped flows in real-time (Cilium clusters)
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --since 1m

# Calico — verify policy enforcement
calicoctl get networkpolicy -n jahez-prod -o wide

# Audit: find all "allow-all" leaks
kubectl get netpol --all-namespaces -o json | \
  jq '.items[] | select(.spec.ingress[]?.from == null and .spec.ingress != null) | .metadata.name'

      The 4-step rollout playbook

      1. Audit the matrix. Document every flow before writing a single policy. (See §P1 for the format.)
      2. Apply default-deny in audit/observe mode first. Cilium and Calico both support audit mode that logs without enforcing — run for a week, find missing flows.
      3. Roll out namespace-by-namespace. Start with the lowest-risk NS (e.g., a dev environment), then platform NS (monitoring), then your core production NS.
      4. Add CI gates. Every PR adding a Deployment must add a corresponding NetworkPolicy or fail the build. Kyverno / OPA Gatekeeper enforces this.
      You're done. You now have the full mental model, the API surface, the patterns, and a complete production-grade microservices project. The next step is to take the YAMLs in §P3–P10 and adapt them to your real label schema and namespaces.
